Mehta, J. 
 
1. Heard. 
2. Leave granted. 
3. The efficacy of medical care is inseparable from 
the trust and respect reposed in the doctors and 
nurses. This enduring truth finds eloquent 
expression in the following verse from  the Suśruta 
Saṃ hitā1:- 
 
1 Suśruta Saṃ hitā Sūtrasthāna 29.52/2-53/1. 

--- Page 31 ---
2 
 
“न स ससध्यसि वैद्यो वा गृहे यस्य न पूज्यिे ।  
भवने पूज्यिे वासप यस्य वैद्यः स ससध्यसि ॥” 
 
4. In its literal sense, the verse conveys that a 
physician does not succeed in a house where he is 
not respected; where the physician is respected, his 
treatment succeeds. Though expressed in the 
language of an ancient medical tradition, the 
principle underlying the verse retains undimini shed 
relevance even today. 
5. Few responsibilities in a civilised society are as 
profound as that entrusted to a doctor. The special 
place accorded to the medical profession flows from 
the very nature of the service it renders to humanity. 
It concerns human life, human dignity and the 
alleviation of human suffering. A doctor is, therefore, 
required to bring to the discharge of his or her duties 
not merely knowledge and technical competence, but 
also sound judgment, patience, composure and 
compassion. The responsibility is consequently o f a 
character that extends beyond the mere provision of 
a professional service. 

--- Page 32 ---
3 
 
6. It is this unique character of the profession that 
distinguishes the relationship between a doctor and 
a patient from an ordinary commercial or service 
relationship. A patient does not merely engage a 
professional for the performance of a task; he places 
his health and, in serious cases, his very life in the 
hands of the doctor. The relationship is thus founded 
upon a degree of trust that cannot be measured 
merely by the professional service rendered or the 
remuneration received.  The ancient Roman Stoic 
philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca aptly expressed 
the thought, while the physician is paid for his 
professional service, gratitude remains owed for the 
kindness and care that transcend the service itself .2 
The observation aptly recognises that the confidence, 
reassurance and humanity accompanying medical 
care form an integral part of the relationship between 
the doctor and the patient. 
7. The weight of this responsibility is brought into 
sharpest relief in the actual practice of medicine. 
Within a hospital, and particularly in an emergency, 
a doctor may be required to assess a patient, make 
 
2 Lucius Annaeus Seneca, De Beneficiis (On Benefits), Book VI , available 
at: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3794/3794-h/3794-h.htm . 

--- Page 33 ---
4 
 
critical decisions and commence treatment within 
moments, often without the benefit of complete 
information. The decision so taken may bear directly 
upon the life and well -being of the patient. The 
discharge of such responsibility necessarily requires 
the physician to remain composed, focused and free 
to exercise independent professional judgment. 
8. An environment conducive to the discharge of 
such a responsibility is, therefore, not a matter of 
convenience for the medical professional. It is a 
condition necessary for the proper delivery of medical 
care. A doctor cannot reasonably be expected to 
exercise sound and independent judgment while 
labouring under the apprehension of physical 
violence, intimidation or coercion. The safety and 
dignity of the medical professional are consequently 
not matters of personal privilege . They are the 
safeguards which serve the larger public interest in 
ensuring that medical care is rendered with the 
concentration, composure and judgment that the 
profession demands. 
9. This does not place medical professionals 
beyond scrutiny or accountability. A patient or his 
family remains entitled to question the treatment 

--- Page 34 ---
5 
 
provided, complain of negligence or delay, seek 
investigation into an adverse outcome and pursue 
such remedies as are available in law. Indeed, the 
availability of these lawful avenues is essential to 
ensuring accountability within the medical 
profession.  
10. What the law cannot countenance is the 
substitution of these remedies by threat, violence and 
coercion. Physical violence, intimidation or coercion 
cannot become a means of expressing dissatisfaction 
with medical treatment, securing compliance with a 
demand or raising grievance for an adverse medical 
outcome. A grievance, however genuine, does not 
confer a licence to resort to violence. To permit such 
conduct would not merely imperil the individual 
doctor. It would undermine the very conditions in 
which medical professionals are required to make 
decisions upon which the life and health of patients 
may depend. Any patronage to such activities would 
alter the civil society in one run by outlaws.

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION 
47. We have given our thoughtful consideration to 
the submissions advanced at bar and have carefully 
gone through the impugned order and the material 
placed on record. 
48. Democracy confers power through the ballot, 
but the exercise of that power remains subject to the 
discipline of law. It is, therefore, a matter of serious 
concern when persons occupying elected office begin 
to perceive the mandate of the people as a source  of 
personal authority and unbridled power and, in the 
process, assume for themse lves a position to 
command, intimidate or even enforce their own will. 
49. The constitutional order draws a clear line 
between authority conferred by law and influence 
exercised by an individual. An elected representative 
is entrusted with the responsibility of serving the 
public and strengthening the institutions through 
which g rievances are addressed and justice is 
administered. He/She cannot supplant those 
institutions by assuming the role of the police, the 

--- Page 49 ---
20 
 
administrator or the Court. The use of personal 
influence to secure compliance through fear or 
intimidation has consequences extending beyond the 
immediate victim and carries the potential to erode 
public confidence in the rule of law itself. 
50. The concern assumes greater significance when 
the persons subjected to such conduct are medical 
professionals entrusted with the care of the health 
and well -being of citizens. These professionals 
discharge onerous duties  in circumstances which 
frequently involve vulnerable patients, medical 
emergencies and decisions requiring instantaneous 
professional judgment and composure. An 
atmosphere of fear or insecurity within a healthcare 
institution can have consequences extending beyond 
the individual medical officer concerned, by 
impairing the safe and effective delivery of medical 
care. Those en trusted with protecting the health of 
others cannot themselves be placed in a position 
where they are compelled to discharge their 
professional responsibilities under fear, intimidation 
or apprehension. 
51. In the conspectus of the aforesaid  
circumstances, we have no hesitation in observing 

--- Page 50 ---
21 
 
that any attempt to intimate or assault medical 
professionals, while discharging duties entrusted to 
them in the interest of public health, cannot be 
tolerated, much less at the hands of persons holding 
elected office or for that matter any other person. An 
elected representative, by virtue of the office 
entrusted to him, bears a heightened responsibility 
to uphold the authority of law and to conduct himself 
in a manner that reinforces public confidence in 
public institutions. Resort to violence against medical 
professionals by a person occupying such office is, 
therefore, particularly grave, as it not only imperils 
the safety and dignity of those entrusted with the care 
of patients, but also undermines the very 
responsibility attached to public office to uphold, 
rather than undermine, the rule of law. The authority 
conferred by an elected office can never furnish a 
basis for disregarding the legal restraints that bind 
every citizen.  
52. Incidents such as the one at hand inflict 
deleterious effects on the peace and tranquility of the 
society at large and also create disruption of public 
order. The fact remains that pursuant to respondent 
Nos.1 to 4 having been granted indulgence of bail, 

--- Page 51 ---
22 
 
one more incident of similar nature happened in 
Palghar, Maharashtra, where doctors and hospital 
staff were subjected to high-handedness and assault 
at the hands of political functionaries. It is asserted 
that when the hospital staff attempted to intervene, 
one of the perpetrators slapped a receptionist  and 
threatened a woman employee. Crucially, the alleged 
assailants also belong to a  political organization. 
Though constituting an independent cause of action 
on its own facts, this occurrence fortifies the 
apprehension regarding the sense of insecurity 
prevailing in medical fraternity. 
53. It is against the foregoing backdrop that we are 
called upon to examine the exercise of discretion  by 
the Courts below in favour of respondent Nos.1 to 4. 
The question before us is not merely whether 
respondent Nos.1 to 4 ought to remain at liberty 
pending trial, but whether the favourable exercise of 
discretion, given the totality of the material available 
on record, suffers from perversity or non-application 
of mind. 
54. We find considerable force in  the submission 
that the approach adopted by the High Court in its 
orders dated 18 th July, 2026 and 7 th August, 2026, 

--- Page 52 ---
23 
 
reflect an irreconcilable approach on key 
considerations crucial to exercising discretion in the 
matter of bail. In its suo moto order dated 18th July, 
2026, the High Court had, prima facie, observed that 
the learned Magistrate could not have granted bail to 
the respondent Nos.1 to 4 having regard, inter alia, to 
the nature of the allegations and the brazen assault 
upon doctors while they were discharging their 
duties. It was on the basis of such prima facie 
assessment that the High Court stayed the operation 
of the orders granting bail.  
55. Having thus intervened and taken the view that 
the orders of the learned Magistrate suffered from 
serious infirmity, the High Court while passing the 
impugned order proceeded to enlarge respondent 
Nos.1 to 4 on bail, though subject to conditions, 
principally on the consideration that they had 
furnished details of their place of residence outside 
the State of Maharashtra, the period of custody 
undergone by them, the substantial progress made 
in the investigation and the likelihood of completion 
of forensic analysis shortly. 
56. What is conspicuously absent from the 
impugned order is any finding as to what intervening 

--- Page 53 ---
24 
 
circumstance had occurred between the two orders 
so as to displace the prima facie view earlier taken by 
the High Court. The mere passage of time in custody, 
progress in investigation or the anticipated 
completion of forensic analysis, without anything 
further, does not explain how the circumstances 
which had earlier weighed with the Hi gh Court had 
ceased to operate or had otherwise lost their 
significance. The impugned order does not undertake 
any such assessment. 
57. The position that emerges on a holistic view is 
that the two orders, despite being rendered in quick 
succession in the same cause and concerning the 
same respondents, proceed upon fundamentally 
conflicting principles bearing upon the entitlement to 
bail. 
58. In our considered view, once the High Court had 
itself found sufficient prima facie evidence to stay the 
orders granting bail and to require respondent No.1-
Ramesh to surrender, any subsequent departure 
from that position necessarily called for cogent and 
discernible reasons. The impugned order, in our view, 
falls short of such an examination. 

--- Page 54 ---
25 
 
59. This assumes greater significance in view of the 
criminal antecedents attributed to respondent No.1-
Ramesh. The criminal antecedents of an accused 
assume particular significance while considering an 
application for bail, especially where the material on 
record indicates a pattern of repeated involvement in 
criminal activities. In the case of habitual offenders , 
such antecedents constitute a material circumstance 
which cannot be disregarded while exercising judicial 
discretion in the matter of bail. Failure to take such 
antecedents into consideration, where they bear 
upon the assessment of the likelihood of repetition of 
criminal conduct, interference with the course of 
justice or intimidation of witnesses, renders the 
exercise of discretion vulnerable to interference by 
the courts. This Court in Ash Mohammad v. Shiv 
Raj Singh & Anr. 14, underscored that the criminal 
antecedents of an accused are a relevant 
consideration while deciding an application for bail 
and observed as follows:-  
“30. We may usefully state that when the 
citizens are scared to lead a peaceful life and 
this kind of offences usher in an 
impediment in establishment of orderly 
society, the duty of the court becomes more 
 
14 (2012) 9 SCC 446. 

--- Page 55 ---
26 
 
pronounced and the burden is heavy. There 
should have been proper analysis of the 
criminal antecedents. Needless to say, 
imposition of conditions is subsequent to 
the order admitting an accused to bail. The 
question should be posed whether the 
accused deserves to be enlarged on bail 
or not and only thereafter issue of 
imposing conditions would arise. We do 
not deny for a moment that period of 
custody is a relevant factor but 
simultaneously the totality of  
circumstances and the criminal 
antecedents are also to be weighed. They 
are to be weighed in the scale of 
collective cry and desire. The societal 
concern has to be kept in view in 
juxtaposition of individual liberty.  
Regard being had to the said parameter we 
are inclined to think that the social concern 
in the case at hand deserves to be given 
priority over lifting the restriction on liberty 
of the accused.” 
                                   (Emphasis Supplied) 
 
60. In the present case, the Courts below have failed 
to accord due consideration to the criminal 
antecedents of accused respondents, in particular 
respondent No.1-Ramesh, against whom 18 criminal 
cases are stated to have been registered, including 
cases involving serious offences punishable under 
Sections 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
Such antecedents were a material cir cumstance 
bearing upon the exercise of discretion in the matter 

--- Page 56 ---
27 
 
of bail and could not have been brushed aside 
without due consideration. 
61. We are conscious that respondent No.1-Ramesh 
has secured acquittal/discharge in 16 criminal 
proceedings. At the same time, the nature of the 
allegations levelled against him and the overall 
circumstances in which his involvement has been 
alleged cannot be lost sight of. The apprehension that 
the influence exercised by him may have had a 
bearing upon the course of such trials cannot be 
wholly ruled out. This circumstance assumes vital 
importance in the present case, particularly when 
material witnesses are required to testify against him.  
62. Furthermore, this Court cannot lose sight of the 
statutory consequences contemplated under Section 
13(1)(a) of the MMCA, 1949, which provides for 
removal of a Councilor from office upon his being 
found guilty of misconduct in the discharge of his 
duties or of any disgraceful cond uct during his 
current term or the immediately preceding term of 
office. The statutory consequences that may ensue 
from the conduct attributed to respondent No.1 -
Ramesh constitute a relevant circumstance which 

--- Page 57 ---
28 
 
cannot be divorced from the overall consideration of 
the case. 
63. The r espondent No.1 -Ramesh continued to 
remain admitted in the prison ward of the District 
Civil Hospital, Thane, throughout his police custody 
remand from 10 th to 13 th July, 2026 and thereafter 
during his judicial custody, thereby substantially 
avoiding confinement in prison . Significantly, 
immediately upon issuance of the release memo 
pursuant to the order granting bail on 15 th July, 
2026, he sought discharge from the hospital. The 
aforesaid conduct, viewed in its entirety, raises a 
serious concern regarding the manner in which the 
influence attached to his position was utilised to 
circumvent the effective operation of the custod ial 
process. 
64. The order granting bail to respondent Nos. 2 to 
4 proceeds substantially on the principle of parity 
with respondent No.1 -Ramesh. Once the very 
foundation upon which respondent No.1 -Ramesh 
was granted the indulgence of bail is found to be 
unsustainable, respondent Nos.2 to 4 cannot claim 
an independent entitlement to the same relief merely 
on the ground of parity. 

--- Page 58 ---
29 
 
65. We also find that the High Court while restoring 
the order(s) granting bail to respondent Nos.1 to 4, 
though subject to conditions, did not accord due 
consideration to the wider impact of the conduct 
attributed to respondent Nos.1 to 4 upon the medical 
fraternity.  
66. The material on record indicates that the 
incident had caused such fear and apprehension 
amongst the victim doctors that they were 
constrained to tender their resignations. This 
circumstance was not merely incidental to the 
individual allegations; it was d irectly relevant to the 
apprehension of intimidation and the ability of 
medical professionals to discharge their duties 
without fear or insecurity. The effect of the prejudicial 
conduct of the accused upon  the functioning of the 
healthcare institution and the confidence of medical 
professionals, therefore, warranted due 
consideration while exercising discretion in the 
matter of bail.  
67. This Court is further of the considered opinion 
that, notwithstanding that respondent Nos.1 to 4 are 
currently in judicial custody, the facts and 
circumstances of the case warrant an evaluation by 

--- Page 59 ---
30 
 
the State Government, in accordance with law, as to 
whether the provisions of the applicable preventive 
detention laws are attracted.  The competent 
authority shall independently examine the matter on 
its own merits, having due regard to the statutory 
requirements governing preventive detention and the 
material circumstances bearing upon the necessity 
for such action, so as to instil a sense of security and 
confidence amongst the medical fraternity and to 
ensure that medical professionals are able to 
discharge their duties without fear or apprehension. 
68. In view of the aforesaid, we find that the High 
Court erred in exercising its discretion in favour of 
respondent Nos.1 to 4. By ignoring material 
circumstances vital to the adjudication of bail , 
specifically the criminal antecedents of the 
respondents, the influence wielded by respondent 
No.1-Ramesh, and the profound impact of the offence 
on the medical fraternity , the civil servants and the 
society at large, the impugned order enlarging them 
on bail cannot be sustained. 
69. We clarify that none of the observations made 
hereinabove shall be construed as according any 
sanction to members of the medical fraternity to 

--- Page 60 ---
31 
 
indulge in dereliction or negligence in the discharge 
of their duties. Any such instance, however, shall be 
dealt with strictly in accordance with law and the 
extant guidelines governing the same. 
70. Before parting with the matter, we may note 
that the present incident cannot be viewed in 
isolation from the larger concern which arises when 
persons occupying elected office resort to force, 
intimidation or other extra -legal means in dealing 
with citizens  or public functionaries. Instances of 
such conduct have been reported from different parts 
of the country. While each such incident must 
necessarily be examined on its own facts and in 
accordance with law, the recurrence of allegations 
involving elected r epresentatives assuming, or 
seeking to assume, authority beyond that conferred 
by law is a matter which cannot be viewed with 
indifference. An elected office carries with it a 
corresponding obligation to respect the rule of law 
and the institutions through which grievances are to 
be addressed. The authority derived from the 
electoral mandate cannot be permitted to become a 
substitute for the authority of law. No person, 
howsoever high the office held, can claim supremacy 

--- Page 61 ---
32 
 
over the discipline of law. The legitimacy of public 
authority ultimately rests not upon the power to 
command, but upon the obligation to remain within 
the bounds of law  and serve the nation . It is this 
distinction that must remain inviolable in a 
constitutional democracy. 
CONCLUSION  
71. As an upshot of the aforesaid discussion, we are 
of the considered view that the present case warrants 
exercise of the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court 
under Article 136 of the Constitution of India. The 
impugned order, accordingly, cannot be sustained 
and is hereby set aside insofar it restores the order(s) 
granting bail to respondent Nos.1 to 4, subject to the 
conditions stipulated therein. 
72. Consequently, the bail granted to respondent 
Nos.1 to 4 stands cancelled. The respondent Nos.1 to 
4 shall surrender before the trial Court concerned 
before 5th October, 2026, failing which the trial Court 
concerned shall be at liberty to cancel their bail 
bonds and take all necessary steps, in accordance 
with law, to secure their custody for the remainder of 
the trial. It is, however, clarified that in the event of 
any materi al change in circumstances, respondent 

--- Page 62 ---
33 
 
Nos.1 to 4 would be at liberty to renew their prayer 
for bail before the appropriate forum, in accordance 
with law. 
73. The directions issued by the High Court in 
paragraphs 9 to 13 of the impugned order shall 
remain undisturbed, save and except the direction 
requiring the trial Court to conclude the trial within 
three months from the date of framing of charges. We 
direct t he Special Fast Track Court , constituted 
pursuant to the directions of the High Court , shall 
endeavour to conclude the trial as expeditiously as 
possible and, in any event, not later than six months 
from the date of presentation of the present order.  
74. We also direct the prosecution to carefully 
assess the list of witnesses proposed to be examined 
and, wherever permissible in law, to curtail or 
dispense with the examination of such witnesses 
whose evidence may not be essential for the just 
adjudication of the case, so as to ensure that the trial 
proceeds expeditiously without compromising the 
fairness of the proceedings. 
75. In the overall factual matrix of the present case, 
and having regard to the fact that the prosecution 
case rests substantially upon the testimony of 

--- Page 63 ---
34 
 
doctors and hospital staff, we direct the trial Court 
concerned to ensure that all material witnesses are 
afforded adequate protection throughout the trial. 
The trial Court shall, in terms of Section 9 of the 
Maharashtra Witness Protection and Security Act, 
2017, and the law laid down by this Court in 
Mahender Chawla  & Ors.  v. Union of India  & 
Ors.15, remain vigilant to any apprehension of threat, 
intimidation or coercion  and, wherever the 
circumstances so warrant, pass appropriate orders 
directing the District Administration/Superintendent 
of Police to extend requisite protective measures, so 
as to ensure that the witnesses are able to depose 
freely and without fear or external influence. 
76. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. 
77. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand 
disposed of. 
….……………………J. 
                            (VIKRAM NATH) 
 
 
...…………………….J.

1. The first thing that we enquired with the learned Amicus today
was whether our directions as contained in paras 40, 41, 42 and 43
respectively issued vide our order dated 15 th September, 2026 have
been complied with or not. 
2. In reply to our aforesaid question, the learned Amicus brought
to our notice that he has addressed one letter dated 19th September,
2026 to the Chief Secretary, Government of NCT of Delhi bringing to
his notice the directions issued by this Court referred to above
and for its due compliance. However, according to the learned
Amicus, he has not heard anything at the end of the Chief Secretary
till this date.  We remind the Chief Secretary of our directions.
The directions read thus: 
“40. The Ld. Amicus brought to our notice that there is a need
for taking steps to ensure safe pedestrian crossing on the
Mathura Road [Near Delhi High Court Junction and National
Zoological Park] as number of officials and litigants approach
the Delhi High Court and have to face difficulties while
crossing the road. Further, children and parents visit the
National Zoological Park. 
41.  In  our  order  dated  07.10.2025,  we  had  observed  as
follows:- 
“35.6 The amicus has also submitted that there is a
need to assess the requirement of further pedestrian
crossings, especially where there is high pedestrian
volume crossing the streets. One can give example of
the road crossing at the Delhi High Court and the
National Zoological Garden on Mathura Road where
every day thousands of employees/ litigants/ lawyers/
children/ families cross the road, without any red
light or foot over bridge or any traffic calming
measure, putting their lives at risk………………….…. We
direct that first priority be given to the road
crossing at the Delhi High Court and the National
Zoological  Garden  on  the  Mathura  Road.  Let  the

--- Page 72 ---
7
needful be done at the earliest and the work be
completed within seven months from today.” 
42. Today, when the matter was taken up, the Ld. Amicus draws
our attention to the fact that though one pedestrian crossing
red light had been installed, it remains non- functional on
various  occasions.  The  Ld.  Amicus  has  also  made  some
suggestions regarding installation of synchronized red lights
at two places along with speed limiting measures like rumble
strips and electronic enforcement mechanism for safety of
pedestrians. 
43. We direct the Union of India and the Delhi Government

We direct the Central Government and Delhi Government to

necessary compliance report be filed by MoRTH and the Chief

3. We direct the Chief Secretary to file a report as regards
compliance of the directions contained in our order dated 15 th

4. If our directions have not been complied with so far, the

5. We have been monitoring this litigation by now over a period

IA No.33035 of 2021:- 
1. In this application, the learned Amicus has prayed for the

“i) Pass an appropriate writ or order or direction to the

electronic monitoring and enforcement of road safety on

--- Page 74 ---
9
the State Highways SHs), prominent corridors and main
roads in the cities within the State with the necessary
follow up action for the traffic violations.”
2. Section 136A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 provides for
electronic monitoring and enforcement of road safety.
3. Section 136A reads thus:-
“136A. Electronic monitoring and enforcement of road safety. 
(1) The State Government shall ensure electronic monitoring
and enforcement of road safety in the manner provided under
sub- section (2) on national highways, state highways, roads
or in any urban city within a State which has a population up
to such limits as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
2) The Central Government shall make rules for the electronic
monitoring and enforcement of road safety including speed
cameras, closed-circuit television cameras, speed guns, body
wearable cameras and such other technology.”
4. The learned Amicus brought to our notice the Order passed by
this  Court  dated  2nd September,  2024  and  20 th January,  2025
respectively. The learned Amicus also brought to our notice the
affidavit  filed  by  MoRTH  dated  13th  February,  2026.  In  the
application, information has been furnished as regards the accident
statistics contained in the MoRTH Report “Road Accidents in India
2024”. 
5. In the aforesaid context, we direct all the States/Union
Territories to forthwith implement the Standard Operating Procedure
(SOP) dated 28 th October, 2025 prepared by the Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways, Government of India (for short, “the
MoRTH). We direct the States/UTs to ensure due compliance of
Section 136A of the Act, 1988 read with Rule 167A of the Rules,
1989. We also direct MoRTH to file their affidavit indicating due
compliance, how they propose to duly comply with the provisions of
Section 136A and in this regard the Authority shall also provide a
specific time-line. We also direct the States/ UTs to implement the
SOP and notify E-Enforcement Sites as mandated by the S.O.P.,
finalize  device  procurement,  deployment  and  calibration
arrangements. 
6. The  National  Road  Safety  Board  (for  short,  “the  NRSB”)
constituted under Section 215B of the Act, 1988 is also directed to

--- Page 75 ---
10
monitor the E-enforcement. We want to convey something to the
States/UTs/Authorities in a plain and simple manner. It is not just
sufficient to keep issuing e-challans to the person who is alleged
to have violated the provisions of the Act. Police may issue
thousands and lakhs of such e-challans but the question is how do
you recover the fine as sought to be imposed by way of those e-
challans. We are informed by the learned amicus as well as the
applicant appearing-in-person Mr. K.C. Jain that the States/UTs
have to recover Rs.49,194.05 Crore approximately towards the e-
challans issued over a period of time. We are also informed that so
far an amount of Rs.26,175.05 Crore has been recovered. What we
want to convey in simple words is that the Authorities need to work
at the ground level having regard to the ground realities. 
7. Ordinarily, once an e-challan is issued, the same is sent to
the concerned territorial Court for recovery of the fine. The
person against whom e-challan is issued has to appear and he makes
the payment of the fine in the Court concerned. There are e-courts
also in this regard. 
8. However, what is expected of the Authorities insofar as
effective implementation of recovery of fine etc. is concerned is
to freeze the online services for vehicles which have outstanding
amounts. The Authorities shall bar from renewing registration
certificate, issuing duplicate registration certificate and also
shall not entertain any request for updating owner's address etc.
The authorities shall also deny fitness certificate until all
pending traffic fines are entirely cleared and further there should
be blacklisting of the vehicle concerned on the Parivahan Portal.
This will come in the way of the person concerned if he wants to
sell his vehicle. The authorities should also proceed to block
ownership transfer. For multiple violations, the driving license
shall be suspended from renewal and measures shall also be taken to
suspend the driving license which may be in force. What is most
important is that no Center should be permitted to issue PUC
certificate. 

--- Page 76 ---
11
9. We invite the attention of the authorities to the amended Rule
21(25) of the Rules, 1989. This amended Rule has been brought into
force with effect from 2026. It provides that the acts by a holder
of a driving licence shall constitute nuisance or danger to the
public,  namely  commission  of  five  or  more  offences  or
contraventions of the provisions of the Act or these rules, in a
period of one year commencing on and from the 1 st January, 2026
provided that no offence or contravention recorded in any previous
one year period shall be taken into account for determining
offences or contravention in any subsequent one year period.
10. We also direct that let there be random checking of the
vehicles and if it is found that the e-challan issued has not been
abided or honored, necessary steps shall be taken to impound the
vehicle itself. 
11. The States/Union Territories/Authorities shall also take into

IA 233571 of 2025:-
1. In this application, the applicant has, inter alia, pointed
out  that  overloading  is  not  a  mere  revenue  or  regulatory
infraction; it is a direct and officially recognized road safety
hazard.

--- Page 78 ---
13
2. An overloaded goods vehicle suffers increased momentum and
braking distance, heightened risk of brake failure, tire blowout
and rollover, reduced steering control and vehicle stability.
3. At  times,  the  excess  axle  load  may  also  cause
disproportionately greater damage to the road surface, creating a
continuing hazard for all road users.
4. In this regard, our attention has been drawn to Sections
113(3) and 114 of the Act 1988, respectively.
5. The applicant has prayed for the following directions:-
“(i) Compulsory Off-loading of Excess Load: MORTH, NHAI, the
States/Union  Territories  and  the  concerned  road-owning
authorities/concessionaires may be directed to ensure that no
transport  vehicle  found  carrying  load  in  excess  of  the
permissible limit, as specified by the Central Government
under  Section  58  of  the  Motor  Vehicles  Act,  1988,  is
permitted to cross or proceed beyond the point of detection-
whether  a  toll/fee  plaza,  check-  post  or  any  other
enforcement  point  until  the  excess  load  is  removed  in
accordance with the proviso to Section 194(1) of the Motor
Vehicles Act, 1988.
For this purpose, the SOP finalised by NHAI and made part of
the Kerala High Court's order dated 19.02.2026 in WP (C) No.
44116 of 2023 (P.B. Satheesh v. UOI & Ors.) may also be
directed to be implemented uniformly across the country in
respect of National Highways and State Highways.
(ii) Statutory Obligations Not Substituted by Payment of
Fee/Penalty: MoRTH, NHAI, the States/Union Territories and
the concerned road- owning authorities/concessionaires may be
directed to ensure that payment of additional fee under Rule
10 of the National Highways Fee (Determination of Rates and
Collection) Rules, 2008, or payment/imposition of penalty
under Section 194(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, shall
not be treated as a substitute for compliance with the
independent statutory obligations under Sections 113, 114 and
194 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, Section 8B of the
National Highways Act, 1956, and other applicable provisions
of law.
(iii) Integration with Electronic Enforcement: MORTH, NHAI,
the States/Union Territories and the concerned road-owning
authorities/concessionaires  may  be  directed  to  integrate
Weigh-in- Motion/weighbridge systems with the Toll Management
System and the electronic enforcement mechanism contemplated
under Section 136A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 read with
Rule 167A of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, and to
ensure interoperability of such systems across States/UTs, so
that enforcement against overloading is not defeated merely
because a vehicle is registered in, or moves into, another
State/UT.

--- Page 79 ---
14
(iv)  Police  Assistance  for  Enforcement:  The  States/Union
Territories  may  be  directed  to  ensure  requisite  police
assistance  to  NHAI,  road-owning  authorities  and  their
authorised officers/concessionaires/toll operators, wherever
required,  for  preventing  an  overloaded  vehicle  from
proceeding  until  the  excess  load  is  removed  and  for
maintaining  law  and  order  during  such  enforcement.  The
States/UTs may further be directed to consider establishing
dedicated police/enforcement units for National and State
Highways, including toll/fee plazas, for effective prevention
and enforcement against the movement of overloaded transport
vehicles.
(v) Periodic Compliance and Accident-Data Reporting: MoRTH,
NHAI and the States/Union Territories may be directed to
furnish, on a quarterly basis, data regarding: (a) overloaded
vehicles detected; (b) challans/proceedings initiated; (c)
vehicles from which excess load was actually removed before
being permitted to proceed; (d) instances of non-functional
weighing  equipment  and  corrective  action  taken;  and  (e)
action taken where overloaded vehicles were permitted to
proceed contrary to law. Such reporting may also include
accident data involving overloaded vehicles, to the extent
captured through iRAD/eDAR or any successor platform. The
consolidated data may be placed before the National Road
Safety Board (NRSB) for scrutiny and periodic review, and
thereafter placed before this Hon'ble Court along with the
NRSB's observations/recommendations and made available in the
public domain.
6. We order accordingly.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This dispute concerning the partition of Property No. 54, Friends
Colony (East), New Delhi, carries a protracted and chequered
history dating back to a civil suit instituted in 1988. Following
a preliminary decree in 1997, a final judgment and decree was
passed in 2007, which mandated that the property be auctioned and
the sale proceeds apportioned among the respective shareholders. 
2. During  the  execution  proceedings,  the  petitioners  sought
exclusive physical possession and partition of their 50% share by
metes and bounds. To achieve this, they attempted to place
reliance on an order passed on 05.11.2019 by a Division Bench of
the High Court wherein, it was stated that it would be open to
the executing Court to explore all possibilities of securing to
the parties their respective shares, as determined by the final
decree, not limited to the sale of the suit property.

--- Page 89 ---
3
3. Arguing that the order dated 05.11.2019 had modified the final
decree's strict mandate for an auction sale, the petitioners
herein filed an execution petition before the High Court. The
Single Judge of the High Court firmly rejected this vide an order
dated 15.02.2023, observing that a decree for sale cannot be
bypassed.  The  petitioners  challenged  this  decision  in  an
Execution First Appeal, which the Division Bench of the High
Court ultimately dismissed  vide the impugned judgment dated
01.05.2024. Aggrieved by the same, the petitioners are before us.
4. Upon the matter reaching this Court, we passed an initial order
on  04.10.2024  appointing  Ms.  Sanya  Shukla  as  the  Advocate
Commissioner to inspect the premises alongside an architect and
structural engineer to comprehensively assess the feasibility of
physically  dividing  the  property and,  thereafter,  submit  a
report.
5. Upon perusing the report submitted by the Advocate Commissioner,
prepared  in  consultation  with  the  architect  and  structural
engineer, and after hearing the learned senior counsel for the
parties, this Court had arrived at the conclusion that a physical
partition of the property by metes and bounds into four distinct
shares was structurally unfeasible because any such attempt would
not  only  compromise  the  existing  superstructure,  but  also
severely destroy the intrinsic value and utility of the plot,

--- Page 90 ---
4
thereby rendering the prospect of physical division entirely
futile.
6. Hence, a cknowledging the futility of physical division, this
Court, after hearing all the concerned parties, directed a fresh
public auction vide order dated 10.09.2025. We also recorded the
strict undertaking of Respondent No. 1 to hand over vacant
possession within one month of the sale's confirmation. The
verbatim extract of the order dated 10.09.2025 is as follows: 
“We have heard the learned senior counsel appearing for the
petitioners and respondents at length. 
This  case  has  got  a  chequered  history.  Notwithstanding  the
preliminary decree followed by the final decree, on a trivial
issue as to whether the suit property can be partitioned or be put
for sale, the parties have been dragging on the litigation. 
Incidentally, one more matter is pending before the High Court, as
the widow of one of the defendants to the suit seeks to contend
that the earlier so-called consent, cannot be taken note of, and
therefore, she is entitled to a 25 per cent share in the suit
property. Suffice it is to state that her grievance is only
limited, with respect to the proportionate percentage constituting
her so-called share. In other words, she has no objection for
either partition or sale of the suit property to be adopted. For
the aforesaid reasons, her presence is not required. We have been
informed that she is no more and her legal heirs are not available
before us. 
We are of the considered view that an attempt can be made afresh,
to bring the entire suit property for sale by way of an auction.
We also take note of the submission made by the learned counsel
appearing for the respondent No.1, that no obstruction whatsoever

--- Page 91 ---
5
would be made or created against the proposed sale, and in any
event, after the confirmation of sale and within a period of one
month thereafter, the said respondent would handover the vacant
possession  of  the  concerned  suit  premises  to  the  intending
purchaser.
The aforesaid statement stands recorded. 
In such view of the matter, we request Ms. Sanya Shukla, the
learned Advocate Commissioner to make a publication in a leading
English newspaper, namely, ‘The Times of India', and apart from
that in two more Hindi newspapers having a wide circulation in the
NCT of Delhi. 
Both the parties are at liberty to approach the learned Advocate
Commissioner, so as to facilitate third parties to participate in
the proposed auction. The learned Advocate Commissioner is at
liberty to conduct an auction, after receiving and scrutinizing
the offers from various parties, but shall not confirm the sale
without the leave of this Court. The needful will have to be done,
within a period of six weeks, from the date of receipt of a copy
of this order. 
A total sum of Rs.10,00,000/- shall be paid to the learned
Advocate Commissioner, of which Rs.5,00,000/- shall be the fees of
the learned Advocate Commissioner, and the remaining Rs.5,00,000/-
would be for the purpose of conducting the auction. The said
amount i.e. Rs.10,00,000/- will have to be borne equally by the
petitioner(s) and respondent(s).
The learned Advocate Commissioner, is at liberty to impose such
terms and conditions as may be necessary, while facilitating and
conducting the auction. For the aforesaid purpose, she can also
get relevant suggestions from the parties.
We also make it clear that the fixing of reserve price is left to
the discretion of the learned Advocate Commissioner.”

--- Page 92 ---
6
7. To facilitate the auction mechanism, we subsequently directed the
Registry,  vide order dated 17.03.2026 , to receive the earnest
money  deposit  from  the  auction  which  was proposed  to  be
conducted. 
8. The public auction was successfully conducted by the Advocate
Commissioner  on  17.06.2026.  A  bidding  consortium  comprising
Scindia Investments Private Limited and Gupta Machine Tools
Private  Limited  participated  and  emerged  as  the  successful
highest bidder, submitting a bid of Rs. 232,50,00,000/- (Rupees
Two Hundred Thirty-Two Crores and Fifty Lakhs). It may be noted
that the successful consortium has duly complied with all terms
by    depositing the entire purchase consideration with the
Registry of this Court.
9. After the successful completion of auction, an initial attempt
was made by the petitioners to try and modify our order dated
10.09.2025 directing an auction. This court,  vide order dated
29.07.2026,  was  not  inclined  to  modify  the  order  dated
10.09.2025, as the said order had been passed after hearing all
the concerned parties. 
10. Furthermore,  vide our orders dated 29.07.2026 and 11.08.2026,
this Court has, in fact, extended extraordinary opportunities to
the petitioners to either match the successful bid or bring
prospective bidders of their own with a higher offer. We even

--- Page 93 ---
7
granted a leeway in allowing the new intending purchaser (ALTO
Housing  LLP)  to  deduct  the  50%  share  pertaining  to  the
petitioners and directed it to deposit only the remaining amount
by 31.08.2026 to facilitate an open court bidding. We explicitly
clarified in our order dated 11.08.2026 as follows: “if the
deposit is not made on or before 31.08.2026, the sale will stand
confirmed in favour of the purchaser who has already deposited
the money.” However, as a matter of fact, the intending purchaser
(ALTO Housing LLP) has failed to deposit the said amount before
the Registry of this Court by 31.08.2026.
11. Today, i.e. 10.09.2026, yet another attempt has been made by the
learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners, relying on annexed
communications  addressed  to  the  Advocate  Commissioner  and
subsequent developments, to contend that the auction proceeding
is  illegal and ought not to be confirmed. The primary basis for
this contention was an attempt to argue that the auction process
had allegedly undervalued the property, as evidenced by the
petitioners bringing forward a new intending purchaser (ALTO
Housing LLP) offering Rs. 250 crores.
12. It is quite unfortunate that such a contention is being made
repeatedly at the instance of the petitioners, despite multiple
opportunities and leeways having been extended by this Court to
the petitioners. E ven today, despite our earlier order  dated
11.08.2026  fixing  a  specific  time  limit  for the  intending

--- Page 94 ---
8
purchaser (ALTO Housing LLP) to make a  deposit before the
Registry of this Court , we have granted yet another opportunity
to the learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner s to
ensure that the  intending purchaser  (ALTO Housing LLP)  would
deposit 50% of the sale consideration that they are willing to
offer.  However, it is submitted that the same would not be
possible.
13. Hence, when viewed from any angle, the petitioners and their
prospective buyers have miserably failed to deposit the required
sums or sustain a viable alternative. The objections raised by
the  petitioners against  the  concluded  auction  process  are,
therefore, devoid of merit and merely attempts at prolonging the
inevitable. 
14. In such view of the matter, t he sale of the subject property is,
hereby, confirmed in favour of the successful bidding consortium,
which has already deposited the entire bid amount of Rs.232.50
crores before the Registry of this Court.
15. This Court is now seized of Interlocutory Application No. 193170
of 2026, preferred by the successful auction purchasers, a
bidding  consortium,  comprising  Scindia  Investments  Private
Limited (Applicant No. 1) and Gupta Machine Tools Private Limited
(Applicant No. 2). The applicants  in the said  Interlocutory
Application, upon confirmation of sale, seek specific directions

--- Page 95 ---
9
regarding the execution and registration of the sale deeds for
Property No. 54, Friends Colony (East), New Delhi.
16. As aforementioned, the applicants/consortium members have already
strictly complied with the terms of the auction and this Court's
directives by depositing the entire purchase consideration of
Rs.232,50,00,000/- (Rupees Two Hundred Thirty-Two Crores and
Fifty Lakhs) with the Registry on 24.06.2026.
17. Per the Joint Bidding Agreement dated 08.06.2026 executed between
the consortium members, the capital contributions and future
ownership of the land parcels are apportioned strictly in the
ratio  of  63.57%  for  Scindia  Investments  Private  Limited
(Applicant No. 1) and 36.43% for Gupta Machine Tools Private
Limited (Applicant No. 2).  In this context, it is submitted on
behalf of the said applicants/consortium members that issuing a
single, undivided joint title deed would necessitate a subsequent
partition deed, triggering additional financial burdens such as
stamp duty and registration charges. It is also submitted that an
undivided title would severely prejudice their ability to raise
independent development loans, create clean commercial mortgages,
and secure necessary municipal approvals, including mutations
from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi.
18. We find merit in these submissions. Executing separate title
deeds for the demarcated portions neither prejudices any party to

--- Page 96 ---
10
the main litigation nor alters the gross consideration receivable
by the co-owners of the subject property.
19. Accordingly, I.A. No. 193170 of 2026 is allowed to the extent
prayed for regarding the sale deeds and the following directions
are issued:
a. The learned counsel appearing for the  Advocate Commissioner
is empowered and directed to execute, sign, and register two
separate and distinct Sale Deeds directly in favour of the
applicants/consortium members as follows:
i. Sale Deed 1: To be executed in favour of Scindia
Investments  Private  Limited  for  a  physically
mapped  and  demarcated  portion  measuring
approximately  2,450  square  yards,  representing
63.57% of the gross land area.
ii. Sale Deed 2: To be executed in  favour of Gupta
Machine Tools Private Limited for a physically
mapped  and  demarcated  portion  measuring
approximately  1,404  square  yards,  representing
36.43% of the gross land area.
b. It is made clear that the entirety of the applicable stamp
duty,  registration  fees,  transfer  duties,  corporation

--- Page 97 ---
11
surcharges, and any incidental statutory charges leviable on
both separate Sale Deeds shall be borne exclusively by the
applicants/consortium  members  in  accordance  with  their
internal proportions.
c. No portion of the stamp duty or registration expenses shall
be deducted from or adjusted against the gross auction
consideration of Rs. 232,50,00,000/- deposited with the
Registry.
d. In terms of the applicable provisions of the Income Tax Act,
it is stated that a statutory deduction of 1% Tax Deducted
at Source (TDS) is required to be made upon the transfer of
immovable property. Since the entire gross purchase price of
Rs. 232,50,00,000/- is lying deposited before the Registry
of this Court, the Registry, in co-ordination with the
learned counsel appearing for the Advocate Commissioner, is
directed to deduct 1% TDS at the time of the release and
disbursement of the respective shares of the purchase price
to the four co-owners. 
e. The Registry, in co-ordination with the learned  counsel
appearing for the Advocate Commissioner, shall ensure that
the TDS so deducted is duly deposited with the Income Tax
Department against the respective Permanent Account Numbers

--- Page 98 ---
12
(PANs) of the four co-owners, and the corresponding TDS
certificates (Form 16B) are promptly furnished to them.
f. The Registry, after deducting TDS in the above-mentioned
manner, is directed to disburse the net sale consideration,
in co-ordination with the learned counsel appearing for the
Advocate Commissioner, as follows:
i. 31.218% shall be disbursed to Mr. Bishwajeet Singh
(Petitioner No. 1 herein).
ii. 18.782%  shall  be  disbursed  to  the  Legal
Representative(s)  of  Late  Mrs.  Vijay  Kumari
(Petitioner No. 2 herein).
iii. 25%  shall  be  disbursed  equally  to  the  Legal
Representatives  of  Late  Mr.  Bikramjit  Singh
(Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 herein).
iv. With respect to the remaining 25% share, as recorded in
this Court's order dated 10.09.2025, the widow of
Defendant No. 2 (Late Mrs. Madhuri Singh), who had
claimed a 25% share, has passed away, and her legal
heirs are not presently before this Court. Therefore,
the Registry is directed to retain the 25% share
corresponding to her branch and invest the same in a

--- Page 99 ---
13
short-term,  interest-bearing  fixed  deposit  with  a
nationalized bank. The release of this 25% share shall
remain subject to the final determination of her legal
heirs  and  the  outcome  of  the  related  proceedings
pending before the High Court. 
g. A sum of Rs. 2,00,000/- (Two Lakhs) shall be paid to the
learned counsel appearing for the Advocate Commissioner for
the  efforts  to  be  undertaken  to  give  effect  to  the
directions passed by this Court in this order. The said sum
shall be borne by the four (4) shareholders in proportion to
their respective shareholding.
h. Insofar as delivery of vacant possession of the subject
property  is  concerned,  t his  Court  vide order  dated
10.09.2025 had formally recorded the express undertaking of
Respondent No. 1, who is said to be in actual physical
occupancy of the premises, to hand over complete vacant
possession to the incoming purchaser within a period of one
month from the date of final sale confirmation.  In terms of
the said undertaking, Respondent No. 1, and any person
claiming through or under him, is directed to hand over
peaceful, vacant, and physical possession of the entire
Subject Property to the authorized representatives of the
applicants/consortium members , within one month from the
date of receipt of a copy of this order.

--- Page 100 ---
14
i. In the event of any failure or default on the part of the
occupants  to  hand  over  vacant  possession  within  the
stipulated  timeframe,  the  local  police  authorities,
including the Station House Officer (SHO) having territorial
jurisdiction over Friends Colony (East), New Delhi, shall
provide all necessary police assistance to enforce the
immediate delivery of vacant physical possession to the
applicants/consortium members upon written request from the
learned counsel appearing for the Advocate Commissioner.
j. Upon the delivery of physical possession, the applicants/
consortium members are granted leave to level and demolish
the existing superstructure standing on the Subject Property
at their own cost, risk, and expense, prior to the formal
administrative  registration  of  the  deeds,  strictly  in
conformity  with  local  municipal  and  environmental
regulations.
20. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of, in the aforesaid
terms.
21. IA No.193912/2026 and IA no.191544/2026 for impleadment stand
allowed in view of this order.

--- Page 101 ---

22. IA No.209715/2026 stands disposed of in view of order dated
29.07.2026 passed by this Court.

O R D E R 
1.     The three applications, i.e., (i) I.A. No. 139335 of 2026 , 
filed by Applicants - Ms. Lauleen Kaur Bhalla and Mr. Jagvinder 
Bhalla, who are the complainants in F.I.R. No.0275 of 2019 and 
F.I.R. No.0274 of 2019, Police Station Kasna, Uttar Pradesh; (ii) 
I.A. No.196507 of 2026, filed by the State of Uttar Pradesh; and 
(iii) I.A. No.266450 of 2026, filed by M/s Translite Scaffolding 
Limited, the original complainant in F.I.R. No.353 of 2015, seek, 
in substance, an overlapping relief: de-clubbing/de-tagging of 
FIRs, relating to the “Grand Venice”/“Grand Venezia” project, 
Greater Noida.   
2.      The first application (I.A. No. 139335 of 2026) seeks the 
de-clubbing/de-tagging of F.I.R. Nos. 0274 of 2019 and 0275 of 
2019, or alternatively to modify the order dated 12.05.2022 and 
declare either FIR No. 0274/2019 or FIR No. 0275/2019 or any 
other allottee’s FIR (other than FIR No. 353/2015) as the 
principal FIR. Simultaneously, the other two applications (I.A. 
No. 196507 of 2026 and I.A. No. 266450 of 2026) seek to de-
club/de-tag the F.I.R. No. 353 of 2015 , Police Station Kasna, 
Gautam Budh Nagar, from the cluster of FIRs, or substitution of 

--- Page 117 ---
Page 3 of 13 
 
F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 as the principal/lead F.I.R. by another 
F.I.R. forming part of the cluster. Though notice was not issued 
in I.A. No. 266450 of 2026, a similar prayer has been made 
therein. The other two IAs have been heard extensively, and 
accordingly all three aforesaid IAs are being disposed of by this 
common order.    
3.      A brief reference to the background facts is necessary. The 
Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 242 of 2019 was instituted by the original 
petitioner, Mr. Satinder Singh Bhasin, under Article 32 of the 
Constitution, inter alia  praying for consolidation of the 
numerous FIRs registered against him  in the State of Uttar 
Pradesh and the National Capital Territory of Delhi , in relation 
to the Grand Venice project, lodged principally at the instance of 
allottees/investors of the project.  By order dated 12.05.2022, 
this Court, in W.P. (Crl.) No. 242 of 2019 , recording the broad 
consensus of learned counsel appearing for the parties, directed 
that the said F.I.R.s be clubbed with F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 dated 
09.06.2015 (registered under Sections 406 and 420 of the Indian 
Penal Code at Police Station Kasna, Gautam Budh Nagar, at the 
instance of M/s Translite Scaffolding Limited), which, being first 
in point of time, was designated as the principal/lead F.I.R. for 

--- Page 118 ---
Page 4 of 13 
 
administrative convenience and to avoid multiplicity of 
proceedings, with liberty to the Investigating Officer therein to 
file a composite/supplementary charge -sheet incorporating the 
material collected in the course of investigation of the other 
cases. By the judgment dated 08.08.2023, passed in W.P.(Crl.) 
No. 242 of 2019,  this Court disposed of the writ petition, 
clarifying that the direction for transfer and clubbing of the 
F.I.R.s would continue to operate as the final order, and that the 
trial would proceed from the stage of the  filing of the  
supplementary charge-sheet.  
4.     It may also be noted that in the very same writ petition, 
the original petitioner, Mr. Satinder Singh Bhasin, had sought 
the prayer of bail in respect of the F.I.R.s referred to therein. 
Accordingly, this Court, by order dated 06.11.2019 in W.P.(Crl.) 
No. 242 of 2019, granted bail to the petitioner, subject to certain 
conditions imposed therein. It was upon breach and non -
compliance of the said conditions imposed vide order dated 
06.11.2019 that the M.A.s came to be filed.   
5.     M.A. No.239 of 2024 was filed by the allottees of the Grand 
Venice project, seeking cancellation of the bail earlier granted to 

--- Page 119 ---
Page 5 of 13 
 
the original petitioner. The said application was allowed by a 
detailed judgment dated 02.04.2026, passed in M.A. No. 239 of 
2024 in W.P.(Crl.) No. 242 of 2019, whereby the petitioner’s bail 
was cancelled for breach of the conditions imposed. Paragraph 
124 of the said judgment recorded that it would be open to any 
party to move an appropriate application before this Court on 
the issue of clubbing/de -clubbing of the F.I.R.s, and that any 
such appl ication would be decided on its own merits. It is 
pursuant to this liberty that the present applications have been 
filed. The aforementioned paragraph 124 has been reproduced 
as follows:  
“124. Another issue that has been raised by the 
petitioner is that the present two -judge Bench lacks the 
jurisdiction to modify or alter the orders clubbing the 
subject FIRs dated 12.05.2022 and 08.08.2023, as it 
was passed by a three -judge Bench. While we are n ot 
delving into this issue in depth as we are concerned with 
the cancellation of bail at this stage, however, we find 
reason to agree with the submission of Mr. Gopal 
Sankaranarayanan, learned senior counsel on this 
aspect. It has been submitted that on oc casions, 2-judge 
Benches of this Court have modified or altered 3 -judge 
Bench decisions, for instance: Arjun Gopal v. Union of 
India and All India Judges Association. Needless to add, 
we clarify that it is open for any party to move an 
appropriate applicat ion before this Court on the issue of 
clubbing/de-clubbing of FIRs. Any such application, if so 
made, shall be decided on its own merits.”  
 

--- Page 120 ---
Page 6 of 13 
 
6.     Learned counsel for Applicants/Ms. Lauleen Kaur Bhalla 
and Mr. Jagvinder Bhalla, and learned counsel appearing for the 
State of Uttar Pradesh, submit, in substance, that: (i) F.I.R. 
No.353 of 2015 arises out of a commercial claim by a vendor for 
non-payment of dues and is unconnected, factually and legally, 
with the allegations of cheating, forgery, criminal breach of trust 
and criminal conspiracy levelled by the several home -
buyers/allottees of the project; (ii) the continued clubbing of the 
allottees’ F.I.R.s with F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 has enabled  the 
original petitioner to project the allottees’ grievances as civil 
disputes and to obtain interim orders, including an order of the 
High Court keeping the trial in abeyance , thereby impeding 
investigation and trial in the allottees’ F.I.R.s.  
7.     A substantially similar grievance has been voiced by M/s 
Translite Scaffolding Limited, the original complainant in F.I.R. 
No.353 of 2015 itself. It is submitted on its behalf that the said 
F.I.R. arises out of a distinct commercial transaction concerning 
unpaid rental dues and non -return of scaffolding material 
supplied for the Grand Venice project, and has no connection 
with the allotment -related allegations levelled by the other 
complainants; that the designation of F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 as 

--- Page 121 ---
Page 7 of 13 
 
the principal/lead F.I.R. has been relied upon by the original 
petitioner to contend, before various fora, that the stay earlier 
operating in the proceedings arising from F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 
extends to, and is determinative of the status of, other 
unconnected F.I.R.s clubbed with it; and that the applicant has, 
in the interregnum, also acquired an independent grievance in 
its capacity as an allottee, which it wishes to pursue on its own 
footing. It is accordingly prayed that F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 be de-
tagged from the cluster and be removed as the principal/lead 
F.I.R. 
8.    These submissions have been seriously contested by learned 
counsel appearing for the original petitioner, whose detailed 
reply raises, in substance, two principal objections:  
It is firstly contended that the applications are not 
maintainable inasmuch as they seek, by way of miscellaneous 
applications filed in an already-disposed writ petition, to unsettle 
the very relief of consolidation that was granted in exercise of 
this Court’s jurisdic tion under Article 142 of the Constitution 
and subsequently made absolute by this Court vide judgment 
dated 08.08.2023  in W.P.(Crl.) No. 242/2019.  It has been 

--- Page 122 ---
Page 8 of 13 
 
accordingly contended that such a final direction, once merged 
in the judgment disposing of the writ petition, can be varied only 
in review or curative jurisdiction and not by a Bench of 
coordinate or lesser strength in collateral proceedings, and that 
the liberty granted in p aragraph 124 of the judgment dated 
02.04.2026, wherein the bail of the original petitioner was 
cancelled, was confined to the context of the bail -cancellation 
proceedings then under consideration and cannot be read as a 
license to reopen the consolidation framework at large.    
It is secondly argued that no demonstrable prejudice has 
in fact resulted from the clubbing, inasmuch as a charge -sheet 
has already been filed in F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 and the Section 
482 Cr.P.C. petition, seeking to quash the proceedings of Case 
No. 1559 of 2019, arising out of Case Crime No. 353 of 2015,  
that had earlier occasioned a stay of the connected proceedings 
has since been dismissed by the High Court on 09.04.2026, 
clearing the way for the trial to proceed.  
9.     We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused 
the material on record, including the orders dated 12.05.2022 , 
passed in W.P.(Crl.) No. 242/2019,  and the order dated 

--- Page 123 ---
Page 9 of 13 
 
08.08.2023, passed in W.P.(Crl.) No. 242/2019  and the 
judgment dated 02.04.2026, passed in M.A. No. 239 of 2024 in 
W.P.(Crl.) No. 242 of 2019.  
10. At the outset, we consider it appropriate to record that 
the clubbing of the several subsequent F.I.R.s with the first F.I.R. 
No.353 of 2015 as the principal F.I.R. was a case -management 
arrangement made by this Court in the peculiar facts of the 
earlier writ petition concerning a single real -estate project, 
lodging of a very large number of F.I.R.s, and complainants 
spread across two States, i.e., Uttar Pradesh and NCT of Delhi, 
with the object of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings and 
enabling coordinated investigation and monitoring. That 
arrangement was subsequently made absolute upon final 
disposal of the writ petition.  Be that as it may, as the Writ 
Petition is already disposed of, it will not be appropriate to review 
the same now. However, that will not preclude this Court from 
clarifying the earlier order , without making any substantial 
alterations to it, if it is so required to dispel any confusion or 
doubts.  

--- Page 124 ---
Page 10 of 13 
 
11.     What has been genuinely and consistently urged by the 
applicants, including by the very complainant in F.I.R. No.353 
of 2015, is an apprehension that the administrative clubbing of 
a totally  unconnected commercial dispute with a set of 
subsequent F.I.R.s alleging grave offences of cheating and 
forgery against home -buyers has come to be construed, or is 
capable of being construed, as having the effect of making the 
progress of one contingent upon the other, or of one stay in one 
order or proceeding engulfing unrelated proceedings. That was 
never the object of the consolidation directed by this Court, and 
it is necessary that this position be placed beyond doubt.  
12. We accordingly clarify that the clubbing of the several 
F.I.R.s pertaining to the Grand Venice/Grand Venezia project 
with F.I.R. No.353 of 2015, as directed vide orders dated 
12.05.2022, passed in W.P.(Crl.) No. 242/2019  was, and 
remains, an arrangement for administrative coordination, and 
does not have the effect of fusing the several F.I.R.s into a 
composite offence or of subordinating the trial, or any interim 
order, in one to the trial or outcome of the lead F.I.R. No. 353 of 
2015, arising as it does out of a commercial claim distinct in 
nature, origin, and evidence from the allegations levelled by the 

--- Page 125 ---
Page 11 of 13 
 
home-buyers/allottees, shall be dealt with and tried strictly on 
its own merits, on the basis of the evidence gathered in the 
investigation and the charge-sheet(s) relatable to it. Equally, the 
several other F.I.R.s lodged by the home-buyers/allottees of the 
project shall each be dealt with and tried strictly on their own 
merits, on the basis of the material collected in the 
investigation/charge-sheet relatable to each such F.I.R. 
13. It is further clarified that: 
(a)      The pendency, progress or outcome of, and any interim or 
interlocutory order (including any order of stay) passed in F.I.R. 
No.353 of 2015 or the proceedings arising therefrom, shall have 
no bearing, procedural or substantive , upon the investigation, 
trial or disposal of the other F.I.R.s forming part of the 
consolidated cluster, and vice versa, as the FIR No. 353 of 2015 
stands on a totally different footing than the remaining FIRs.  
(b)     No finding, observation or order made in the proceedings 
relatable to one F.I.R. shall be treated as binding upon, or as 
constituting a precondition for, the proceedings relatable to any 
other F.I.R. forming part of the said cluster; 

--- Page 126 ---
Page 12 of 13 
 
(c)  The order dated 12.05.2022 passed by this Court in 
W.P.(Crl.) No. 242/2019, cannot mean to divest the trial court of 
the power contained in Chapter XVIII of the Bharatiya Nagarik 
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (corresponding to the provisions on 
joinder of charg es and joint or separate trial contained in 
Chapter XVII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Having 
said that, the concerned trial court shall be at liberty to exercise 
power under the provisions contained in Chapter XVIII of the 
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 or such other 
provision as may be applicable, to frame separate charges, order 
joint or separate trial, or otherwise regulate the trial of the 
several F.I.R.s and accused persons, as may be found necessary 
in the interest of a fair, expeditious and non -prejudicial trial, it 
being well settled that provisions relating to joinder of charges 
and joint trial are enabling in nature, to be applied having regard 
to the facts of each case, and are not to operate so as to delay or 
obstruct the trial of any set of F.I.R.s; 
(d)     Nothing herein shall preclude the concerned trial court 
from proceeding with, and disposing of, the trial relatable to any 
F.I.R. or set of F.I.R.s independently of, and without awaiting the 

--- Page 127 ---
Page 13 of 13 
 
outcome of, the proceedings relatable to F.I.R. No.353 of 2015 or 
any other F.I.R. forming part of the cluster. 
14. We clarify that the above directions are issued solely to 
ensure that the administrative arrangement made by this Court 
does not, in its operation, cause prejudice or occasion delay to 
any set of complainants, and are not to be construed as an 
expression of opinion on the merits of the allegations contained 
in any of the F.I.R.s, or on the guilt or innocence of any accused, 
all of which shall be examined by the competent court(s) in 
accordance with law.  
15. We also make it clear that the clarification in this order 
will not prejudice the original petitioner/accused in any manner. 
I.A. No.139335 of 2026, I.A. No.196507 of 2026 and I.A. 
No.266450 of 2026 are accordingly disposed of with the above 
clarification.

O R D E R 
The appeal is by one among the three accused and
the allegation against him was that he held and
restrained the deceased when the 1st accused delivered
multiple stab injuries which resulted in death. The
accused were convicted for offences punishable under
Sections 302 & 341 read with Section 34 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). They were handed down
sentences of rigorous imprisonment for life with a fine
of Rs.5,000/- each, and on default one month simple
imprisonment.
Page 1 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 129 ---
2. The High Court, on an appeal by all the three
accused while upholding the conviction, modified it to
one under Section 304 Part I of the IPC and sentenced
each of them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a
period of ten years. 
3.  Two persons who held the accused while A1
stabbed were both named Mukesh and hence, we refer
to the parties by their status before the Sessions Court.
The overt act was alleged on A1 and the person who
restrained the deceased were A2 and the appellant
herein, who was arrayed as A3. 
4. That  the  death  was  a  homicide  has  been
categorically proved by PW2, the Doctor who conducted
the postmortem examination.  The deceased had seven
ante-mortem injuries in his body, but most of it
lacerations, two contusions, and two incised wounds.
The injuries 6 and 7 were the incised wounds on the
right inguinal region and the right Iliac crest, obviously,
Page 2 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 130 ---
in the area of the under belly at the waist. The 6 th injury
on the right inguinal region, according to PW2 cut
through the femoral vessel artery, the bleeding from
which resulted in the death.  The Doctor was confronted
with the knife which was recovered under Section 27 of
the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and his testimony was
that the weapon shown to him could have definitely
caused the injuries.
5. The prosecution in all, arrayed 11 witnesses of
which PW1 and PW4 were eyewitnesses.  PW5 and PW6
witnesses to the recovery under Section 27.  PW7, the
aunt of the deceased and PW8, a neighbor, both of
them came to the scene of occurrence on hearing the
shouts.  PW9 is the father of the deceased and PW3,
PW10 and PW11 are respectively the Assistant Sub
Inspector (ASI) who registered the FIR, the Head
Constable who took custody of the blood stained clothes
of the deceased and the Sub Inspector who was the
Investigating Officer (I.O).  PW5 and PW6; witnesses to
Page 3 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 131 ---
the recovery under Section 27, denied, any statement
having been made by the accused in their presence
and, also their presence when the knife was recovered,
as narrated by the I.O.  The signatures in the Section 27
statement and the recovery Mahazar were admitted but
their presence was denied. PW4 and PW6 likewise
turned hostile and the eyewitnesses’ testimony that was
relied upon was that of PW1 alone.  
6. PW1 is a person who had close acquaintance with
the deceased and they together were attending the
marriage function of the daughter of one Narayan. They
were having food, served at the function, when A2 is
said to have refused to serve the deceased. The
deceased protested  when a quarrel ensued. A1 who
was also attending the function stood up and slapped
PW1 and started a fight.  PW1 and the deceased in an
attempt to leave the place walked forward when A1
exhorted death with an expletive upon which A1 and A3
caught hold of the deceased. A1 suddenly brandished a
Page 4 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 132 ---
knife and stabbed the deceased near the waist; twice in
the front and twice in the back. On hearing the shouts
of PW1, PW4 came to the scene of occurrence and both
of them together placed the victim on a cot where he
breathed his last.  PW1 is said to have taken the
deceased to the Government Hospital in a tractor and
reported the incident at the Kanad Police Station on the
same night.  As per his testimony, the police also came
to the scene of occurrence within half an hour and he
pointed out the place where the incident occurred.  
7. We  cannot  but  notice  the  very  stark
inconsistencies that were brought out in the cross
examination of the said witness, wherein he again
asserted that the police came on the very same night
and arrested three persons; A1, one Narayan and
Narayan’s relative.  It was also asserted that all the
three were arrested then and there and they were put
in a lockup for the night.  PW1 is also said to have
remained in the police station for the night. He was
Page 5 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 133 ---
confronted with Exhibit P1 and P2, the First Information
Statement (FIS) and the FIR which indicated as per his
own statement that he arrived at 07.30 am on the next
morning and his explanation; reduced to writing, was
that the delay was due to absence of any means of
transport.  PW1 also spoke of injuries on his cheek and
that his clothes were stained with the blood of the
deceased, since he picked up the injured.  Immediately,
we have to notice that PW3, the Doctor who conducted
the postmortem also examined PW1 and found no
injuries on his cheek.  The police had not seized any
blood stained clothes of PW1, for scientific examination.
Strangely enough, PW1 while speaking of having, on the
same night, taken the body to the hospital and reported
at the police station, also spoke of having fainted on
seeing the injured victim. 
8. PW4 who turned hostile was proffered by the
prosecution as an eyewitness.  In cross examination of
PW1, he had stated that when the deceased was
Page 6 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 134 ---
stabbed, he had called out to PW4 who had come
immediately to help him carry the victim to the cot.
However, in cross examination, this was put as an
omission to him under Section 161, the statement given
before the police. Strangely PW4 does not speak of
even the presence of PW4. PW4 spoke of having come
to the scene of occurrence on hearing shouts and saw
the deceased running and falling down on the road.
Since no one picked him up, PW4 called out, when PW7,
the aunt of the deceased came running; together, PW4
and PW7 picked the victim up.  PW4 denied having seen
the incident and hence he was declared hostile.  
9. PW7 also did not speak of the presence of PW1 at
the scene of occurrence. According to her, she ran to
PW4 on hearing him call out and saw the injured victim
and together they picked him up and put him on a cot.
In cross examination, she categorically stated that she
had not stated to the Police, about the presence of PW1,
at the spot.  Hence, PW4 and PW7, witnesses of the
Page 7 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 135 ---
prosecution did not even speak of the presence of PW1
and they did not witness the actual incident. 
 
10. Further suspicion regarding the narration of PW1
arise from the evidence of PW3, the ASI of Kanad Police
Station who registered the FIR on the FIS of PW1. PW3
categorically denied any call having been made to the
police station, as testified by PW1.  PW3 also denied the
police having gone to the scene of occurrence on the
very same night. The arrest of three persons, as
testified by PW1 was also categorically denied by PW3.
According to PW3, as is seen from the FIR, the FIS was
registered at 07.30 am in the morning on the next day,
on the FIS given by PW1. 
11. As is noticed, PW5 and PW6 who are the witnesses
to the confession under Section 27, of the concealment
of a knife and the discovery made at the instance of A1,
had turned hostile on both these counts.  Be that as it
may, PW11 speaks of such recovery having been
effected and even if we believe the same; going back to
Page 8 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 136 ---
PW1’s testimony it has to be noticed that he spoke of
A1 having produced a knife, suddenly and that he did
not see the knife in the hands of PW1. The identification
of the knife by PW1, given the circumstances is very
doubtful. Otherwise, he deposed, he would have
definitely interfered and prevented the assault with a
knife. PW8 and PW9 was proffered by the prosecution to
speak on PW1’s version of what transpired, these
witnesses having come to the scene of occurrence,
immediately after the incident.  PW8 is a neighbor and
PW9 is the father of the deceased. Both of them spoke
of having fainted on seeing the body and regained
consciousness much later. The attempt of PW8 and PW9
to testify about the presence of PW1 at the spot fails to
impress us.  
12. PW1’s presence at the scene of occurrence is
suspect accentuated by the inconsistencies in his
testimony. PW1 also spoke of four stab injuries while
there were only two detected, in the postmortem. The
Page 9 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 137 ---
other witnesses proffered as eyewitnesses turned
hostile and did not even speak of the presence of PW1.
One of the eyewitnesses was confronted with an
omission insofar as PW1’s presence on the scene of
occurrence, as stated by her to the police, which also
stood confirmed by the I.O.  The I.O. also spoke of no
arrest having been made on the same night and the FIR
having been registered on the next day. He also denied
PW1’s statement that he was taken to the police station
on the same night from the hospital and remained at
the police station for the entire night. 
13. A specific suggestion was made to the I.O. that
PW1 was not an eyewitness and that he was forced into
making such a statement, which of course was denied
by the I.O. 
14. On a conspectus of the evidence led at the trial,
we are unable to sustain the conviction and sentence of
the appellant herein.  The conviction and sentence,
Page 10 of 13
Crl. A. No.2913 of 2025

--- Page 138 ---
hence, is set aside. The appellant, if in custody, shall be
released forthwith, if not wanted in any other case and
if released on bail, his bail bonds shall stand cancelled.
15. The appeal stands allowed.  
16.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
