          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This appeal, at the instance of the Securities and Exchange
Board of India (SEBI) arises from the judgment and order passed by
the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) by which the
appeal preferred by SEBI against the order passed by the NCLT,
rejecting the intervention application preferred by SEBI came to be
dismissed.
2. We need not delve much into the facts giving rise to this
litigation between the parties as we are in a position to dispose
of the present appeal on the basis of the consensus which has been
arrived at between all the stakeholders.
3. To  put  it  briefly,  the  appellant  SEBI  received  various
complaints against a company by name Pancard Clubs Limited (PCL)
alleging fraudulent fund mobilization across the country.
4. SEBI initiated auction of all the properties of the company
and in pursuance of the same, and also directed Pancard Clubs
Limited and its Directors to refund the amounts collected from the
investors under an un-registered Collective Investment Schemes
along with returns or not to carry out any Collective Investment
Schemes.
5. SEBI also initiated recovery proceedings against the company
and  its  directors.  According  to  SEBI,  the  company  owes
Rs.7035,00,01,000/- to its investors.
6. It appears that simultaneously, proceedings were initiated
4

--- Page 145 ---
under the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in
Financial Establishments) Act, 1999. Under the provisions of the
Act of 1999, the Government of Maharashtra attached properties of
the concerned company (corporate debtor). 
7. The matter ultimately reached before the NCLT in the form of
Section 7 application filed under the IBC by a group of investors
(respondent nos.3 to 102, respectively).
8. Section 7 application at the instance of these respondents
came to be admitted by the NCLT. In those proceedings before the
NCLT, SEBI moved an impleadment application and prayed that they
may also be heard before proceeding further in the matter. The said
impleadment application came to be rejected by the NCLT. Being
dissatisfied, SEBI went in appeal before the NCLAT and the appeal
also came to be dismissed. 
9. In view of the aforesaid, SEBI is here before us with the
present appeal under Section 62 of the IBC.
10. In the meantime, the Section 7 application culminated in
sanctioning of the Resolution Plan.
11. We  must  clarify  that  there  are  hundreds  of  different
properties owned by the corporate debtor, however, the plan of the
Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) was confined only to nineteen
(19) properties of the corporate debtor. The plan was approved for
Rs.707 crore. In accordance with the terms of the plan, Rs.200
crore were to be paid by the Resolution Applicant over a period of
time and out of Rs.200 crore, Rs.69.80 crore has been paid to the
investors. 
12. In the course of hearing of this appeal, one issue came up
5

--- Page 146 ---
before us whether the valuation of the properties is appropriate or
not  as  undertaken  by  the  adjudicating  authority.  In  such
circumstances, keeping in mind the interest of the investors, we
decided  to  constitute  a  Committee  headed  by  Hon’ble  Justice
Sudhanshu Dhulia, former Judge of this Court. We requested the
Committee to undertake the exercise of ascertaining the correct
valuation of the assets, more particularly, the nineteen (19)
properties which form part of the Resolution Plan.
13. Today, we have a very composite Report of the Committee. We
may incorporate the relevant part of the Report as under:-
“11. After carrying out the aforesaid exercise, the IP has
placed its final report before the Committee. I have perused the
valuation report prepared and, in this regard, the following
observations  are  submitted  with  respect  to  the  properties

814.19 crores.

14. The  Committee  has  concluded  its  Report,  observing  the
following in paras 17 and 18, respectively:-
“17. In  conclusion,  the  Committee  submits  that  the  present
exercise  has  revealed  that  the  asset  base  of  PCL  is  both
substantially larger and structurally more complex than what was
considered during CIRP. There is more to it than meets the eye.
8

--- Page 149 ---
18. Also, the investors were also permitted to file their
representations before the IP, who had to place them before this
Committee. The IP informed the Committee that he has received
certain representations from the investors. The IP Informs the
Committee  that  the  main  concern  of  the  investors  is  quick
recovery of their money. The IP also informs the Committee that
investors are interested in the maximization of the recovery for
investors  and  some  investors  also  highlighted  the  concerns
related to the auction of certain properties by SEBI at an
undervalued price. This is how the IP sums up the representations
received from the investors, which seems logical, though this has
not been stated in his Report.”
15. We heard Mr. Chander Uday Singh and Mr. Pratap Venugopal, the
learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, SEBI, Mr. Navin
Pahwa, the learned senior counsel appearing for the Successful
Resolution Applicant (SRA), Dr. S. Muralidhar, the learned senior
counsel appearing for respondent nos.3 to 102 (investors), Mr.
Vikram Chaudhri, the learned senior counsel appearing for one of
the intervenors, Mr. Sridhar Potraju, the learned senior counsel
appearing for some of the impleaders in I.A. No.167422/2025, Mr.
Ashwin Arun Hirulkar, the learned senior counsel appearing for some
of the other intervenors and Mr. Prashant S. Kenjale, the learned
counsel appearing for a party claiming to be a bona fide purchaser
of one of the properties purchased in the auction conducted by
SEBI, which is a subject matter of Writ Petition before the High
Court on the issue of valuation and Ms. Archana Pathak Dave, the
learned A.S.G., appearing for the Serious Fraud Investigation
Office (SFIO).
16. In the course of today’s hearing manifold contentions were
9

--- Page 150 ---
sought to be raised by both the sides. However, keeping in mind the
paramount consideration, i.e., the interest of the investors, we
have suggested the following and which has been accepted by all the
learned counsel appearing in this matter.
17. We designate Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia, the former
Judge of this Court as the Chairman of the ‘Asset Sale Committee’.
The Committee will consist of one nominee of SEBI, one nominee of
the investigating team under the MPID Act, one nominee from the
side of the investors as may be decided by Justice Sudhanshu
Dhulia. SEBI shall provide all secretarial assistance to the
Committee headed by Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia. 
18. Mr. Navin Pahwa, the learned senior counsel appearing for the
Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) submitted that his client
would like to withdraw from this entire litigation. His client is
ready and willing to take back Rs.69.80 crore which he has already
paid to the investors and over and above, such sum as may be
determined  by  the  Committee  based  on  the  evidence  of  the
expenditure incurred over a period of time in running the company.
19. The Committee shall now prepare a list of all the properties
and start putting those properties to auction. Any objection of any
nature with respect to a particular property may be raised before
the Committee and the Committee shall look into it on its own
merits.
20. The issue about the under valuation at the instance of SEBI,
which is a subject matter of adjudication before the High Court of
Bombay shall also be looked into by the Committee.
21. The client of Mr. Vikram Chaudhri, who claims to be the lawful
10

--- Page 151 ---
owner of one property which is indicated as an asset of the
corporate debtor because the corporate debtor had 22% share in the
company of the client of Mr. Vikram Chaudhri shall also be looked
into by the Committee.
22. At the end of the auction proceedings of all the properties,
whatever amount is fetched from the same, the amount to be paid to
the client of Mr. Navin Pahwa shall be defrayed and also to the
respective investors. It is needless to clarify that whatever
amount the investors have received so far shall be adjusted
accordingly.
23. The Committee shall also make all endeavors to identify the
assets which have been purchased abroad. The SEBI shall put forward
the entire details of these properties before the Justice Sudhanshu
Dhulia Committee and the Committee shall undertake the valuation of
those properties accordingly. In this regard, the Union of India
and other authorities shall render the necessary assistance to the
Committee.
24. The remuneration to be paid to Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia and
other members of the Committee shall be initially borne by SEBI.
Later, this amount can be realized from the funds that may be
collected from the auction proceedings.
25. It shall be open for Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia to fix his own
terms  of  fees/remuneration.  Insofar  as  other  members  of  the
Committee are concerned, an appropriate fee be fixed, if any.
Parties are directed to get in touch with Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia
at the earliest.
26. Insofar as disbursement of funds is concerned, since the
11

--- Page 152 ---
client of Mr. Navin Pahwa is exiting this litigation, priority be
given to him.
27. Since the competent authority under the MPID Act is going to
be a part of the Committee, it shall be bound by all the decisions
taken by the Committee.
28. We make it clear that all the proceedings pending as on date,
shall remain under abeyance till the Committee finishes the entire
exercise. 
29. Registry shall forward one copy of this order to Hon’ble
Mr. Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia at the earliest.
30. The Civil Appeal No.5089 of 2019, titled “SEBI vs. Rohit
Sehgal & Ors.” and Civil Appeal No.20971 of 2017, respectively
shall come up for hearing on 27th November, 2026 at 02:00 P.M. along
with the present appeal to report further progress in the matter.
31. All the intervention applications shall also be listed along
with the aforesaid three appeals.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.             /2026
@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NOS.33517-33518/2026
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR. APPELLANTS
                                VERSUS
YADVENDRA SINGH   RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Based on an anonymous complaint dated 08.11.2024 against
the respondent whereunder it was alleged that he was posting
objectionable  posts  against  the  Government,  Constitutional
Institutions and authorities, the appropriate Government directed the
Director to conduct a preliminary inquiry into the allegations.
Accordingly, a preliminary inquiry was conducted and a report was
forwarded after elucidating the reply from the respondent herein, the
1

--- Page 165 ---
respondent herein was placed under suspension under Rule 4(1) of
the Uttar Pradesh Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal)
Rules, 19991 and disciplinary proceedings under Rule 7 of the Rules
was instituted. He was also attached to the Directorate and
sanctioned subsistence allowance. Challenging the said action, Writ
Application No.7687 of 2025 came to be filed, which came to be
dismissed as withdrawn as he did not choose to pursue his remedy.
On 03.06.2025, chargesheet was issued against the respondent
containing four charges enclosing the annexures thereto. The
Commissioner, Varanasi Division, appointed the Inquiry Officer, and
thereafter, the respondent tendered an unconditional apology for his
objectionable posts on 06.06.2025. Respondent also appeared
before the Inquiry Officer for oral hearing on 14.08.2025, and after
considering the reply given to the chargesheet and the material
placed before him, the Inquiry Officer submitted his report on
24.09.2025 holding that all charges were proved. In the meanwhile,
the respondent had filed another Writ Application No.15072 of 2025
for expeditious conclusion of the departmental proceedings, and as
such, by order dated 07.10.2025, the High Court disposed of the said
Writ Application directing that the proceedings be concluded within a
period of three months.
1  the Rules
2

--- Page 166 ---
4. The aforesaid inquiry report was forwarded to the competent
authority, and a show-cause notice was issued to the respondent as
contemplated under Rule 9(4)of the Rules by granting 15 days' time
to submit his representation. After considering the representation of
the respondent, by order dated 17.01.2026, the order of penalty was
passed whereunder the respondent was reverted to the post of
‘District Backward Class Welfare Officer’ under Rule 3 of the Rules.
5. Challenging the order of reversion, Writ Application No.4037 of
2026 was filed, whereunder the order dated 17.01.2026 was
questioned. On 01.07.2026, the High Court stayed the operation of
the punishment order dated 17.01.2026 on the ground that matter
requires consideration. Subsequently, on 13.08.2026, the order
dated 01.07.2026 was modified and the respondent was allowed to
continue in the post of ‘Deputy Director, Backward Class Welfare’ on
which post he was working when the order dated 17.01.2026 came
to be passed. Due to non-implementation of the said order, contempt
proceedings have been initiated, and it is said to be pending.
Assailing the aforesaid two orders dated 01.07.2026 and 13.08.2026,
the present appeals have been filed.
6. It is the contention of Mr. Rana Mukhopadhyay, learned Senior
Counsel appearing for the appellant(s), that High Court had exceeded
3

--- Page 167 ---
its scope while granting interim relief and directing the restoration of
the respondent to the post held prior to the punishment order and
payment of salary, thereby substantially granting the relief sought for
in the Writ Application itself at the interlocutory stage. He would also
elaborate his submissions by contending that by order dated
01.07.2026, the order of reversion dated 17.01.2026 had only been
stayed and it had neither been set aside or quashed and the
departmental inquiry conducted against the respondent being in
accordance with the prescribed rules, and all the four charges having
been proved in the inquiry, the High Court committed an error in
staying the order dated 17.01.2026, and modifying the said order and
directing the appellant(s) – appropriate Government to revert the
respondent back to the post which he held on the day, the order
reverting the respondent, came to be passed.
7. Per  contra,  Mr.  Sanjeev  Sagar,  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing on behalf of the respondent employee, would support the
impugned order and would submit that inquiry conducted was in utter
disregard to the extant rules, and it is only after examining that there
was no compliance to Rule 7 of the Rules and being satisfied with the
same, the jurisdictional High Court had granted the stay of the order
dated 17.01.2026, and on account of the respondent not having been
4

--- Page 168 ---
put back to the position he held as on that date, the order dated
01.07.2026 came to be modified on 13.08.2026, which orders does
not suffer from any infirmity whatsoever, and as such he has prayed
for rejection of the present appeals. He would also rely upon the
Office Memorandum dated 31.07.2026 passed by the appropriate
Government, which has effectively implemented the order dated
01.07.2026, and as such, he submits that there is no necessity for the
impugned orders being set aside.
8. Having heard the learned Senior Counsels appearing for the
parties and on perusal of the records, prima facie, we notice that the
respondent, by his representation dated 06.06.2025, had tendered an
unconditional apology for the objectionable posts or in other words
admitted his guilt. As to whether this would suffice for the Inquiry
Officer to submit his report holding the charges as proved is an issue
which will have to be thrashed out in the pending Writ Petition by
considering the rival contentions. If this Court were to embark upon
conducting a roving inquiry on the basis of the rival contentions now
raised, it is likely to prejudice the rights of either of the parties in the
pending Writ Application. Hence, we refrain from expressing any
opinion in that regard. The fact remains that respondent, at the time
the impugned order (17.01.2026) came to be passed, was working as
5

--- Page 169 ---
‘Deputy Director, Backward Class Welfare’ and he has been demoted
as ‘District Backward Class Welfare Officer’. In the Writ Application,
the said order was impugned, and the learned judge, by order dated
01.07.2026, stayed the said order vide paragraph No.10. For vacating
the said order, an application has been filed by the appropriate
Government, and undisputedly, the same is still pending. In this
scenario, the High Court ought to have examined either the
continuation of the interim order dated 01.07.2026 or vacating or
modifying or varying the said order.
9. In the background of contempt proceedings having been
initiated for non-implementation of the order dated 01.07.2026, the
appropriate Government seems to have complied with the same by
the Office Memorandum dated 31.07.2026 (Annexure P-5) and
restored his position as that of a “Suspended Deputy Director”, which
was the situation prevailing prior to 17.01.2026 or in other words
respondent came to be placed in the position he held prior to
17.01.2026 namely that of “Suspended Deputy Director”. On this
also, we refrain from expressing any opinion. It is thereafter the High
Court, by the second impugned order dated 13.08.2026, seems to
have virtually granted the main relief, though it is disguised as an
interim relief. It is this process which was undertaken by the High
6

--- Page 170 ---
Court is erroneous and liable to be set aside. Accordingly, we set
aside the order dated 13.08.2026 and grant liberty to both the parties
to urge their contentions before the High Court and the jurisdictional
High Court shall consider the application filed by the appropriate
Government for vacating the order of stay dated 01.07.2026, which is
still pending, and dispose of the said application and/or pass
appropriate orders either vacating or setting aside, or modifying, or
affirming the order dated 01.07.2026 as it deems fit and appropriate
by examining rival claims on merits. On the said issue, we have made
it clear that we have not expressed any opinion, and it is open for
both the parties to urge all grounds in that regard. We hasten to add
that in the light of this order being passed, the contempt proceedings
said to have been initiated by the respondent shall not be proceeded
with till appropriate orders on the stay application has been passed.
Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of. It is needless to state that
in the event of the High Court is of the view that consideration of the
application for vacating the stay would be as good as disposing of the
Writ Application itself, it would be open in the realm of the High Court
to take up the Writ Application itself and dispose of the same
expeditiously alongwith the application for vacating the stay on
merits and in accordance with law. Both parties are at liberty to seek
7

--- Page 171 ---
for pre-ponement of the Writ Application before the jurisdictional High
Court.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
.................J.
  (ARAVIND KUMAR)
.................J.
(VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)
NEW DELHI;

India- Writ Petition [C] No.13029/1985, an order has
been passed on 15.10.2025, by the Bench comprising

involved in both the matters, namely, the present
matter and the M.C. Mehta (supra) are incidental and
overlapping and, therefore, it would be ideal to
hear the matters together.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.5674 of 2026
Jitu @ Jeetu          ...Petitioner
Versus
State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.      ...Respondents
O R D E R
1. The petitioner-accused is before this Court,
challenging the order of the High Court, which
refused to interfere with the compromise entered into
with the victim. The compromise was insofar as an
FIR registered by the victim produced as Annexure P1
dated 06.10.2020 against the petitioner alleging that
she was forced into sexual intercourse from the year
2013 and even afterwards in 2019, after she was
separated from her husband.
Page 1 of 7
SLP(Crl.) No.5674 of 2026

--- Page 195 ---
2. The allegation was also that in 2013, she
permitted the same, on the petitioner promising to
marry  her.  But  later  after  marriage  she  was
threatened with the photos taken when they had a
relationship and subsequently, after she separated
from her husband, again she was engaged on the
pretext of marriage. The High Court found that the
compromise is no reason to quash the FIR; especially
since earlier there was a quash petition filed, which is
also rejected.
3. We were informed by the petitioner’s Counsel
that  the  petitioner  had  married  the  victim  on
31.10.2020 and they had two children and were living
together as a couple. We, hence, directed the
petitioner and the victim to be produced before us.
4. Today both the petitioner and the victim were
personally present before us along with a Sub-
Inspector, Ms. Rajnandini, D-6894 of Police Station
Page 2 of 7
SLP(Crl.) No.5674 of 2026

--- Page 196 ---
Hauz Qazi, Central Delhi. The Sub-Inspector identified
both the petitioner, who is the accused and the
victim. The Sub-Inspector also told us that on enquiry
she has come to know that they were neighbors and
now  are married  and  living together  with  two
children. The Sub-Inspector also submits that the
Certificate of Marriage at the Arya Samaj Mandir
(Trust) has been produced before her, and she
verified the same and found it to be correct. We also
interacted with the couple and the victim has
informed us that the FIR was registered on a wrong
advice.
5. Looking at the facts and circumstances of the
case and especially the fact that the parties are now
married and are living together, we find absolutely no
reason to permit the continuance of the criminal case
lodged against the petitioner; especially noticing that
the FIR of 2020 was registered after a long delay,
making allegations starting from 2013.
Page 3 of 7
SLP(Crl.) No.5674 of 2026

--- Page 197 ---
6. The FIR No.182 of 2020 of Police Station Hauz
Qazi hence stands quashed and there shall be no
further criminal proceedings initiated against the
petitioner herein on that count.
7. The SLP is disposed of.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.   5666 of 2014  
SUPERINTENDING ENGINEER, 
HIRAKUD GENERATION CIRCLE & ANR.
  APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
A. JOGEYA RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6693/2019
AND 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 8102/2014
AND
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 8100/2014
AND
CIVIL APPEAL NO.   8101/2014  
O R D E R
CIVIL APPEAL NO.   5666 of 2014  
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The present appeal is arises out of the order dated
02.09.2013 passed by the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack in
Writ Petition (C) No. 12198 of 2013.
3. The facts of the case reveal that the respondent-
1

--- Page 202 ---
workman was identified by the Labour Court on 20.05.2006 to
be entitled to the benefit of the order of this Court dated
13.08.1985 passed in Civil Appeal Nos. 348 and 349 of 1974,
as  also  the  award  of  interest  from  the  date  of
superannuation of the workman, that is, 01.05.2001.
4. It was urged before the High Court that the workman
had approached the Labour Court for his identification
after a lapse of 20 years, and therefore the management
could not be forced to pay interest as per the subsequent
order dated 09.02.1988 passed by this Court in Civil
Miscellaneous Petition Nos. 10620-10621 of 1987. Other
grounds were also raised in the matter.
5. On behalf of the employee, it was submitted that the
workman is entitled to interest at the rate of 10% per
annum on the arrears amount, which has rightly been awarded
by the Labour Court, and is also entitled to medical
allowance  in  terms  of  the  order  of  this  Court  dated
13.08.1985.
6. The High Court, after hearing both the parties,
observed that even though the workman had submitted his
claim belatedly, directed the employer, keeping in view the
order passed by this Court dated 13.08.1985 in Civil Appeal
Nos. 348 and 349 of 1974 and the subsequent order dated
09.02.1988, to pay the workman arrears along with interest
2

--- Page 203 ---
at the rate of 10% per annum.
7. However, the High Court has categorically held that
the workman shall be entitled to interest from the date he
was identified by the Labour Court, and not from an earlier
date. The High Court has further held that the workman is
entitled to medical allowance payable to employees of the
work-charged establishment of the Central Public Works
Department, keeping in view the order of this Court dated
13.08.1985.
8. This Court does not find any reason to interfere
with  the  impugned  order  passed  by  the  High  Court.
Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6693/2019, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 8102/2014 ,
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 8100/2014 AND CIVIL APPEAL NO.   8101/2014  
1. Learned counsel for the parties fairly submit that
the issues involved in the connected appeals are identical
to the one decided in Civil Appeal No. 5666 of 2014.
2. In view of the order passed in Civil Appeal No. 5666
of 2014, these connected appeals are also dismissed in the
same terms.

of.

Heard Mr. Avishkar Singhvi, learned counsel for
the petitioner-husband and Mr. Sanjoy Ghose, learned
Senior Counsel for the respondent-wife.
2. The respondent-wife is present in Court, duly
identified by her Counsel.
3. Delay condoned.
4. Leave granted.
5. Though, the matter was taken up in the first
half, a prayer was made by learned counsel for the
parties that there may be some scope for settlement
despite mediation having failed. On the second call,
as the terms could not be finalized, we gave further
time and finally, when the matter is taken up, we are
1

--- Page 214 ---
DIARY NO.60105/2025
glad to note that settlement has been arrived at.
6. According  to  the  settlement,  the  appellant-
husband has agreed to pay an amount of Rs.35,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Five Lakhs) by way of a one time
settlement in lieu of grant of divorce by mutual
consent. Further, he is also agreeable to pay a sum
of  Rs.30,00,000/-  (Rupees  Thirty  Lakhs)  for  the
respondent-wife to buy a land of her choice and built
a house on it in the area she desires.
7. The  parties  also  agree  that  the  Court  in
exercise of its jurisdiction and power under Article
142 of the Constitution of India, may dissolve the
marriage  between  the  appellant-husband  and
respondent-wife and grant them divorce by mutual
consent.
8. We have checked up with the respondent-wife, who
is present in Court, with regard to what has been
dictated in this order above. She has stated that she
has  understood  what  has  been  recorded  and  is
agreeable to the same.
9. Having regard to the aforesaid, the appeals are
disposed of in the following terms:
(i) The appellant-husband shall pay a sum of
2

--- Page 215 ---
DIARY NO.60105/2025
Rs.20,00,000/-  (Rupees  Twenty  Lakhs)  to  the
respondent-wife by 31.10.2026.
(ii) Thereafter, installments of Rs.15,00,000/-
(Rupees Fifteen Lakhs) each shall be paid latest
by 30.11.2026, 31.12.2026 and 31.01.2027, taking
the total to Rs.65,00,000/- (Rupees Sixty Five
Lakhs).
(iii)  By exercising our jurisdiction and power
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India,
the parties are granted a decree of divorce by
mutual consent. Registry to draw the decree of
divorce accordingly.
10. We note that upon payment of the entire amount of
Rs.65,00,000/- (Rupees Sixty Five Lakhs), the parties
shall not have any claim whatsoever against each other
as this is the full and final settlement of all dues
inter  se  between the appellant and respondent and
their  son.  However,  we  make  it  clear  that  this
settlement will not have any bearing on whatever
rights the son of the parties shall have on the
appellant, his father on account of his biological
relationship.

five of the appeals have not been decided on

1

--- Page 220 ---
High Court to be decided afresh on merits, the
remaining two matters may also be remitted to the
High  Court.  He  further  submitted  that  the
aforesaid submission is being made based upon the
premise  that  the  allegations  against  the
appellant(s) are overlapping and similar in all
the appeals. 
4. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent(s) submitted that the allegations are
distinct in each appeal and not overlapping. He
submitted that taking note of the fact that this
Court has already taken a view in other similar
matter(s) to remit and decide those appeals on
merits which have been rejected on the ground of
delay, the other two matters would have to be
decided on merits by this Court, as they have
already been decided on merits by the High Court.
5. On going through the records of all the three
matters, we find that the submission advanced by
learned  Standing  Counsel  for  the  State  of
Jharkhand that in two matters being, Criminal
Appeal @ Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.
8802 of 2026 and Criminal Appeal @ Special Leave

2

--- Page 221 ---
Court has decided the prayer for bail on merits is

Court has dismissed the appeal of the respective
accused appellant on the ground of delay. 
6. Considering the submissions made and taking
note of the fact that the present appeals pending
before us arise from orders whereby, the High
Court dismissed the appeal seeking bail as being
delayed, we deem it appropriate to give one more
opportunity to the appellant(s) to argue all the
appeals before the High Court on merits and seek
disposal thereof in accordance with law.
7. In such view of the matter, the impugned
order(s) is/are set aside and the matters are
remitted to the High Court to be decided afresh on
merits and in accordance with law without going
into the question of condonation of delay. We
request the High Court to make an endeavour to
dispose of the said appeals within a period of two
months from the date of receipt of a copy of this
order.
8. All issues are left open to be raised and
argued by the contesting parties.

set aside the impugned order passed by the High

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION  
CIVIL APPEAL NO.8138 OF 2014 
 
VIMAL BINDAL           …APPELLANT 
 
VERSUS 
 
VED PRAKASH KHARBANDA      …RESPONDENT 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. The present civil appeal arises from the judgment and order 
dated 08.03.2013 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New 
Delhi in Regular First Appeal No. 83  of 2007 (hereinafter 
referred to as the “impugned judgment”), whereby the  High 
Court allowed the appeal preferred by the respondent, who was 
the defendant before the learned Additional District Judge, Fast 
Track Court, Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the “Trial Court”), 
set aside the judgment and decree dated 18.11.2006 passed in 
Suit No. 171 of 2006, and dismissed the  suit instituted by the 
appellant for specific performance and possession in respect of 
property bearing No. 53, New Krishna Nagar, Delhi, arising out 
of the agreements to sell dated 05.07.1996 and 22.08.1996. 
 
2. The facts giving rise to the present appeal are as follows: 
2.1. On 05.07.1996, the appellant entered into an agreement 
with the respondent for  purchase of property bearing No. 
53, New Krishna Nagar, Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the 

--- Page 244 ---
C.A. NO.8138/2014  2 
 
“suit property”) for a total sale consideration of Rs. 
13,95,000/- (Rupees Thirteen Lakhs Ninety Five Thousand 
only). An amount of Rs. 1,50,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Fifty 
Thousand only) was paid as earnest money. Thereafter, on 
22.08.1996, another agreement was executed in 
continuation of the earlier agreement and a further amount 
of Rs. 1,70,000 /- (Rupees One Lakh Seventy  Thousand 
only) was paid by the appellant.  
2.2. The time for completion of the transaction was 
subsequently extended and, on  16.10.1996, the 
respondent made an endorsement extending the date for 
completion up to 30.10.1996. The appellant claimed that 
she remained ready and willing to  perform her part of the 
agreement and appeared before the concerned Sub 
Registrar on 30.10.1996 with the balance sale 
consideration. The respondent disputed the  same and 
claimed that the agreement stood cancelled on account of 
the failure of the appellant to perform her obligations. 
2.3. On 31.07.1997, the respondent issued a legal notice 
repudiating the agreement  and claiming forfeiture of the 
amount of Rs. 3,20,000 /- (Rupees Three Lakhs Twenty  
Thousand only) paid by the appellant. The appellant 
thereafter instituted the suit for  specific performance and 
possession on 21.08.1997. 
2.4. By judgment and decree dated 18.11.2006, the Trial Court 
decreed the suit for  specific performance and directed the 
appellant to deposit the balance sale  consideration of Rs. 

--- Page 245 ---
C.A. NO.8138/2014  3 
 
10,75,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs Seventy Five Thousand 
only) within thirty days. The respondent was directed to 
execute and register the sale deed  and hand over vacant 
and peaceful possession of the suit property to the 
appellant. 
2.5. The respondent preferred Regular First Appeal No. 83 of 
2007 before the High  Court. By the impugned judgment 
dated 08.03.2013, the High Court set aside the  judgment 
and decree of the Trial Court and dismissed the suit for 
specific performance and possession. The High Court, 
however, directed refund of the  amount of Rs. 3,20,000 /- 
(Rupees Three Lakhs Twenty Thousand only) to the  
appellant with interest at the rate of 12 per cent per annum. 
 
3. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment dated 08.03.2013, 
whereby the  High Court set aside the decree for specific 
performance passed by the Trial Court and dismissed the suit 
instituted by the appellant, the appellant has  preferred the 
present civil appeal. 
 
4. We have heard Mr. Deepak Raj Singh, learned counsel for the 
appellant, and Mr. Vikas Gupta, learned counsel appointed by 
the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee to represent the 
respondent. The respondent, Mr. Ved Prakash Kharbanda, has 
also appeared in person along with his son, Mr.  Sandeep 
Kharbanda. 
 

--- Page 246 ---
C.A. NO.8138/2014  4 
 
5. Having regard to the long pendency of the dispute and the 
nature of the  controversy, we considered it appropriate to 
explore the possibility of bringing  the litigation to an end and 
putting quietus to the matter. The dispute arises  out of a 
transaction which is nearly three decades old and has remained 
pending before this Court for a considerable period. In such 
circumstances, a mutually acceptable resolution would serve 
the interests of both sides and obviate the need for continuation 
of the litigation. 
6. During the course of hearing, considering the approximate 
current valuation of the suit property, we put to the respondent 
appearing in person an option either to perform the agreement, 
receive an amount of approximately Rs. 3,00,00,000/- (Rupees 
Three Crores only) and vacate the suit property, or to retain the 
suit property upon payment of an amount of Rs. 75,00,000 /- 
(Rupees Seventy Five Lakhs only) to the appellant. The 
respondent expressed his  categorical unwillingness to vacate 
the suit property and opted for the latter course. In view of the 
stand taken by the respondent and with a view to  bringing 
finality to the dispute, we consider it appropriate to dispose of 
the appeal on the aforesaid terms. The amount deposited by the 
appellant with the Registry pursuant to the order dated 
15.07.2013 shall be returned to the appellant along with the 
accrued interest. 
7. In view of the above, the respondent shall pay a sum of Rs. 
75,00,000/- (Rupees Seventy Five Lakhs only) to the appellant 
within a period of one year from today. 

--- Page 247 ---
C.A. NO.8138/2014  5 
 
8. In the event the aforesaid amount is not paid within the 
stipulated period, the appellant shall be at liberty to apply for 
recall of this order and for hearing of the appeal on merits. 
 
9. The impugned judgment dated 08.03.2013 shall stand modified 
to the aforesaid extent. 
 
10. The appeal stands disposed of accordingly. 
 
11. All pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 14020 of 2025)
BHOLA ALIAS MAHESH CHANDRA APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF U.P.        RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out of the impugned order
dated 23.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Criminal Appeal No. 332 of 2026, whereby the
application for bail/suspension of sentence filed by the
appellant was rejected.
3. The facts of the case reveal that the appellant has
been convicted for the offence punishable under Section 412
of the IPC1, and has undergone approximately two years and
two months of the sentence awarded to him.
4. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits
that the looted goods were allegedly recovered at the
instance of the appellant from the premises of the owners
1. Indian Penal Code, 1860
1

--- Page 261 ---
of Om Chemical Tiles Factory. The said factory owners were
also arrayed as co-accused in the case and have been
convicted for the offence punishable under Section 412 of
the IPC. It is submitted that, in the case of the said co-
accused, the High Court has already suspended the sentence
awarded to them. It is, therefore, submitted that the
appellant is also entitled to the benefit of parity.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
has  vehemently  opposed  the  prayer  for  suspension  of
sentence, contending that the appellant is not entitled to
the benefit of parity, as it was the appellant who had
allegedly sold the looted goods to the other co-accused
persons.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
have perused the material available on record. Taking into
consideration the period of incarceration already undergone
by the appellant and the fact that the sentences of the
other co-accused persons, who have also been convicted
under Section 412 of the IPC, have already been suspended,
we are of the view that the appellant is also entitled to
relief on ground of parity.
7. Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the High
Court is set aside.
8. The  execution  of  the  sentence  awarded  to  the
2

--- Page 262 ---
appellant shall remain suspended during the pendency of the
appeal before the High Court, subject to such terms and
conditions as may be imposed by the Trial Court.
9. The High Court is requested to take up and decide
the pending criminal appeal at an early date, preferably
expeditiously.
10. The appeal is allowed in the aforesaid terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.      OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO.5653 OF 2025)
RAJAT CH. KALITA & ANR.                            APPELLANT(S)
A1 SHRI RAJAT CH. KALITA
A2 SHRI PHUKAN DAS
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF ASSAM & ORS.                          RESPONDENT(S)
R1 THE STATE OF ASSAM REP. BY THE PRINCIPAL SECRETARY 
TO THE GOVT. OF ASSAM CO-OPERATIVE DEPARTMENT DISPUR
R2 THE REGISTRAR OF CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES, GOVT. OF ASSAM
R3 THE ASSAM STATE CO-OPERATIVE UNION
R4 THE CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER, ASSAM STATE CO-OPERATIVE UNION
R5 THE PRINCIPAL SECRETARY, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE, DISPUR
O R D E R
Heard  Mr. Kaushik Choudhury, learned counsel for
the petitioners and Mr. Chinmoy Sharma, learned Senior
AAG for the respondent no.1 – State of Assam. 
2. Despite service of notice on respondents no.2 to 5,
there is no appearance on their behalf.
3. Leave granted.
4. The present appeal arises out of a judgment passed
by the Division Bench of the Gauhati High Court dated
1

--- Page 266 ---
17.10.2023 in Writ Appeal No. 168 of 2019, by which the
order dated 25.04.2019 passed by the learned Single
Judge of the Gauhati High Court in W.P.(C) No.2047/2019
holding that no  mandamus can be issued against the
State  of  Assam  for  payment  of  salaries  to  the
appellants herein has been upheld.
5. Learned counsel for the appellants submitted that
the issue got settled inter  se between the parties by
an order dated 24.02.2006 passed by the learned Single
Judge  of  the  Gauhati  High  Court  in  W.P.(C)
No.7086/2005. Thereafter, the Review Petition being
R.A.No.70 of 2006 was also dismissed vide  order dated
04.05.2007  and  challenge  to  the  same  before  the
Division Bench in W.A. No.369/2007 met the same fate by
order dated 10.12.2009.
6. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1-State of
Assam submits that this Court in the case  of State of
Assam  v.  Barak  Upatyaka  D.U.  Karmachari  Sanstha 1 has
held that no such mandamus can be issued.
7. Having considered the matter in depth, we find
that the order impugned cannot be sustained. First and
foremost, the issue with regard to the liability of the
State to make the payment has been settled between the
parties by the order dated 24.02.2006 passed by the
1  (2009) 5 SCC 694
2

--- Page 267 ---
learned  Single  Judge  of  the  Gauhati  High  Court.
Thereafter, even at the level of the Division Bench in
appeal,  the  same  was  upheld  by  the  order  dated
10.12.2009.  The  order  on  which  reliance  has  been
placed, i.e.,  Barak  Upatyaka  D.U.  Karmachari  Sanstha
(supra) is dated 17.03.2009. Thus, the Division Bench
having passed the order nine months after passing of
the  order  by  this  Court  in  Barak  Upatyaka  D.U.
Karmachari  Sanstha  (supra), the State, if it was so
aggrieved, being conscious of this fact, had to file a
review or move before this Court against the order
dated 10.12.2009, more so, for the reason that it was
inter  se  between the parties, i.e., a judgment in
personam. The same not having been done, now at this
stage, we find that the learned Single Judge as also
the  Division  Bench  by  the  order  impugned  have
misdirected  themselves  and  have  reopened  and  gone
behind and, in fact, unsettled the settled position.
8. Accordingly,  the  appeal  is  allowed.  The  order
passed by the learned Single Judge, as upheld by the
Division Bench are set aside. The respondent no.1-State
of Assam is held liable to make the payment in terms of
the order dated 24.02.2006 passed by the Gauhati High
Court in W.P.(C) No.7086 of 2005. Let the appellants be
paid whatever is due to them in accordance with law
3

--- Page 268 ---
without any delay.
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of. 
.....................J.
(AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH)
....................J.
(MANMOHAN)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(s).       OF 2026 
(Arising out of SLP(C) No. 7137/2026) 
 
 
RAMABAI BAPU YEDE & ORS.         APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
RATANBAI LAXMAN YEDE & ORS.          RESPONDENT(S) 
 
ORDER 
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. We have heard Mr. Prasenjit Keswani, learned senior counsel for 
the appellants and Mr. Saksham Maheshwari, learned Advocate-on-record 
for the respondents. 
3. The appellants assail the order dated 27.01.2026 in Civil 
Revision Application No. 707 of 2023 of the High Court of Judicature 
at Bombay in the present Civil Appeal. The appellants are the 
plaintiffs in Special Civil Suit No. 145 of 2016 before the Court of 
the 2nd Joint Civil Judge, Senior Division, Baramati , and the 
respondents are the defendants. 
4.  The defendants have filed an application under Order VII Rule 
11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short, ‘CPC’)  seeking 
rejection of the plaint on the ground that, on a bare perusal of the 
cause of action and the nature of the prayers, the suit is hopelessly 
barred by limitation. The appellants, by filing a counter, explained 
how the cause of action and the prayers survive and are available to 
them in the present litigation. 
5. It is relevant to note that the appellants have also filed an 
application for amendment of plaint to include the following prayers 

--- Page 276 ---
2 
in the plaint: 
“23A-1 A declaration of the Hon'ble Court be 
obtained stating that the judgment dated 15/5/2017 
passed by the Hon'ble Tehsildar Sir, Daund in the 
matter of B.N.D./Application No. 7/2015 regarding 
the suit property is fundamentally void and 
illegal, and therefore it is not binding on the 
Plaintiffs and should be cancelled. 
D) Hollow entries in the names of Defendant Nos. 
1 to 20 have been made in the 7/12 records of the 
suit property. Taking undue advantage of the same, 
Defendant Nos. 1 to 20 should not sell or transfer 
the suit property to any other third parties, nor 
should they change the original nature of the suit 
property in any manner, and an order and decree of 
permanent injunction be passed against the 
Defendants, restraining Defendant Nos. 1 to 20 
themselves or through any other third person, 
servants, agents, heirs or  anyone else, from 
causing any interference or obstruction to the 
peaceful possession and enjoyment of the 
Plaintiffs in the suit property. 
 
23D-1  Until the final judgment of the present 
suit, the judgment dated 15/5/2017 passed by the 
Hon'ble Tehsildar Sir, Daund  in the matter of 
B.N.D./Application No. 7/2015 regarding the suit 
property is fundamentally void and illegal, and as 
per the said order, Defendant Nos. 1 to 4 should 
not take any action regarding handing over 
possession of the suit property by colluding with 
revenue officers, and accordingly, to the peaceful 
possession and enjoyment of the Plaintiffs in the 
said suit property under Clause 1/3  
 
That the Hon'ble Court be pleased to pass an order 
of temporary injunction against Defendant Nos. 1 
to 4 so as not to cause any  
interference/obstruction. 
 
C) Alternatively, if the Hon'ble Court is of the 
opinion that the Defendants are in possession of 
the suit property, then the Hon'ble Court be 
pleased to pass an order directing the Defendants 
to hand over physical and vacant possession of the 
suit property to the Plaintiffs. If necessary, an 
order for handing over vacant possession of the 
suit property be passed through the Hon'ble Court 
or through a Court Commissioner.”  
 
 
6.  The amendment was allowed. Consequently, the amended prayer is 

--- Page 277 ---
3 
also part of the plaint for consideration by the Trial Court. The 
defendants aggrieved by the order of the Trial Court filed Civil 
Revision Application No. 707 of 2023 before the High Court of Bombay. 
The Civil Revision was allowed.  
7. Hence, the Civil Appeal. 
8.  Mr. Prasenjit Keswani, appearing for the appellants, does not 
press the prayers originally made in the plaint. But he limits his 
submissions to the prayer made through amendment, which has been 
excerpted (Supra). The argument is that, under Section 138 of the 
Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966, the aggrieved parties have a 
statutory and independent remedy against the orders made thereunder 
before the Civil Court. 
9.  In the case at hand, through the amended prayer, the appellants 
are assailing the order of the Tehsildar dated 15.05.2017. Therefore, 
it cannot be said that the remedy available to the appellants under 
the said Code can also be rejected on the ground of limitation.  To 
the extent of the amended prayers, if the plaint is rejected, the 
plaintiff will be rendered remediless, and thus this aspect is not 
independently considered by the High Court, but the plaint is rejected 
in its entirety. 
10.  Mr. Saksham Maheshwari, Advocate -on-record, appearing for the 
respondent, objects to the continuance and maintenance of the prayers 
as made, on the ground that the order of the Tehsildar is subject to 
appeal and revision. The suit has been filed before exh austing the 
available statutory remedies. 
11. Alternatively, to avoid complicating the matter, it is argued 
that the pleadings, cause of action and the prayer be confined to  

--- Page 278 ---
4 
the circumstances relevant to the order dated 15.05.2017 of the 
Tehsildar, but not every detail which was relied upon in support of 
the original prayers. 
12.  We have heard the learned counsel and perused the record, 
particularly the order of the Tehsildar. We are of the view that the 
High Court is right in holding that the prayers originally made in 
the plaint do not stand the scrutiny under Order VII Rule 11 CPC and 
rightly rejected the same. B ut rejecting the amended prayer, as 
excerpted above, again could be contrary to the very finding recorded 
by the High Court in the impugned order. The period of limitation is 
not an ex plicit circumstance insofar as amended prayers are 
concerned. On this short ground, to the limited extent of retaining 
the excerpted prayer, the High Court's rejection order is set aside, 
the plaint is restored to that extent, and the Trial Court is directed 
to continue the trial in respect of the prayers. The defendants, if 
have not filed an additional written statement, are granted eight 
(08) weeks’ time from today to file the same.  
13. Hence, the civil appeal is allowed accordingly. 
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Heard Mr. Jayprakash Bansilal Somani and Mr. Abhinav Kumar,
learned counsel for the petitioners and Ms. Aishwarya Bhati,
learned Additional Solicitor General for the respondent no.1-Union
of India assisted by Ms. Sonali Jain, learned counsel.
2. The  issue  involved  in  these  present  petitions  has  been
crystalised in our order dated 12.03.2026. For convenience, the
same is reproduced herein under:-
“…..
2. The main issue involved in the present case(s) relates to
the criteria for selection as a Primary School Teacher in
different languages which required the candidate to have
studied in the said medium from Standard-I till Standard-X.
3. We are convinced that the appropriate criteria for a
person who has to teach the said language should be that
she/he is well conversant with the language, which can only
be possible if right from the very beginning, he/she has
studied in that medium or the subject concerned. However, we
have been informed that the Recruitment Rules were amended
on 11/12/2023 for the post of Primary School Teacher by
which it was notified that the candidate(s) should have
passed  in  the  Hindi/English/Bengali/Telugu  as  one  of
subjects in Class-X in the medium concerned. We find such
amendment to be in the teeth of the object sought to be
achieved and in our tentative view, this is against public
interest as a person who studies a language only for one
year, cannot be allowed to get recruited on a post where
he/she has to teach such subject in a particular language.
4.  Thus, we issue notice to the Union Territory of Andaman
and Nicobar Islands as also to the petitioners, as to why,
the Court may not suo motu strike down such amendments.
….”.
3. Having considered the matter and taking into account the
passage of time, as the recruitment was started in the year 2018
and thereafter, a fresh recruitment had taken place in the year

--- Page 298 ---
4
2023, which resulted in persons having been appointed, who are
working,  balancing  the  equities,  the  present  petitions  stand
disposed of in the following terms:-
(i) the concerned authority shall re-advertise the posts
with regard to the vacancies available afresh. However, the
terms of the advertisement inter alia, will be in accordance
with what has been observed in the order dated 12.03.2026
passed by this Court with regard to the medium in which,
he/she had done his/her schooling till 10th Standard.
(ii) the said exercise be initiated, latest within two
months  from  today  and  completed  within  four  months
thereafter.
(iii) for the purposes of ensuring that the persons, who had
applied for the posts in the year 2018 do not get left out
due to efflux of time having crossed the upper age limit, we
direct that limited to the next exercise, all persons, who
had applied and taken part in the exercise pursuant to the
advertisement published in the year 2018, have crossed the
upper age limit, a one-time relaxation in age would be given
to all such candidates to participate and take part in the
exercise proposed.
4. Before parting, we make it clear that the format of the
application for showing that a candidate fullfills the criteria as
far as the medium of language in which he/she had studied till the
10th Standard is concerned, in terms of our order dated 12.03.2026,
would be such that the entire period the said candidate had

--- Page 299 ---
5
studied, right from 5 th Standard till 10 th Standard, would be
permitted to be furnished by them in  their application form.
5. It  goes  without  saying  that  the  Rules  for  such  fresh
recruitment, if required, be suitably amended/modified in terms of
the directions issued by this Court on 12.03.2026 as quoted above.
The same be done within four weeks from today.
6. After  the  order  was  dictated,  learned  counsel  for  the
applicant in I.A. No.127234 of 2023 submits that on 24.09.2026, he
has withdrawn the said I.A. but in the order dated 24.09.2026
inadvertently, the year of the said I.A. has wrongly been mentioned
inasmuch as, it ought to have been 2023 but has been wrongly typed
as 2026.
7. In view thereof, let the said I.A. indicated in the order
dated 24.09.2026 be read as I.A. No.127234 of 2023 instead of I.A.
No.127234 of 2026.

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant who is arraigned as an accused in FIR No.97 of 2021
registered for the offences punishable under Section 30(a) of the Bihar
Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016, is seeking for grant of anticipatory bail.
4. The case of the prosecution is: acting on a secret information, the
police intercepted a truck bearing Reg. No.JH02L6930 and Bolero bearing
Reg. No. BR26F 8106, near village Sadipur and three persons were
apprehended from the truck and two from the Bolero. 2325 liters of
country made liquor and foreign liquor were found in the truck and 375
liters of country made liquor from the Bolero. The apprehended persons
had disclosed that the consignment had been ordered by Lalaji Singh. The
1                                                                                       SLP(CRL.) NO.17817 OF 2026 

--- Page 301 ---
appellant was not apprehended at the spot. His implication was based
upon as being registered owner of the truck. The trial court had rejected
the anticipatory bail and the High Court has confirmed the said order.
Hence this appeal.
5. Having heard the learned advocates appearing for the parties, we
notice that it is the defence of the appellant that he had sold the truck
under a sale agreement dated 31.05.2020 and the purchaser had become
the owner of the vehicle wef 01.05.2020 as agreed to under the order of
agreement. Hence, the appellant is in no way connected to the alleged
truck or the contraband which came to be seized on 12.05.2021.
6. In the light of the said defence, which requires to be established during
the course of the trial and other co-accused having already been enlarged
on regular bail, we are of the considered view that it is a fit case for
granting anticipatory bail to the appellant.
7. Hence, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on anticipatory bail on such terms and conditions
as the jurisdictional Investigating Officer (IO) may deem fit to impose
including the condition of directing the appellant to appear for further
investigation as and when called upon and to appear before the trial court
on all dates of hearing except when exempted for any specific reason
apart from any other condition he may deem fit and appropriate to
impose.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.531 of 2026
POOJA RANI                                       
Petitioner(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.                          
Respondent(s)
O R D E R
The petitioner is aggrieved with the impugned
order of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at
Chandigarh;  which  we  are  of  the  opinion  is
perfectly in order, especially considering the
manner  in  which  allegations  are  made  of
molestation and sexual intercourse on the promise
of marriage, which are then later settled, by the
sheer  coercion  exerted  on  such  criminal
proceedings  being  initiated  and  continued.
However,  we  intend  to  slightly  modify  the
directions issued.
2. The  petitioner,  a  31-year-old  woman,
registered an FIR on 12.01.2024, alleging that
while she was tending to her brother admitted in
a  hospital,  the  respondent  offered  his
assistance, and on that pretext, became intimate
with her and coerced her into sexual intercourse;
which  even  according  to  her,  she  willingly
complied believing that he would marry her, which
he promised. She also alleged that the parents of
the respondent also met her and there was a sort
of ceremony conducted and then later she was

--- Page 311 ---
2
abandoned. 
3. A settlement was arrived at, in which the
respondent  promised  to  pay  an  amount  of
Rs.9,25,000/-, of which, Rs.4,50,000/- was paid.
The High Court found that the very perusal of the
record  prima  facie  reveals a  mala  fide  case,
especially when the petitioner is a mature woman
who was fully conscious of her act and conduct.
By making allegations of sexual harassment on the
pretext of marriage, she had put into motion the
criminal justice machinery, which according to
the High Court; undermines the sanctity of the
legal process.
4. The  High  Court  observed  that  the  Courts
should not become instruments of undue pressure,
leading to extortion from one party and illegal
enrichment of another. To preserve the integrity
of the criminal justice system, the High Court
set  aside  the  settlement  and  made  it
unenforceable with respect to the balance amounts
payable to the petitioner. The High Court also
directed  that  the  proceedings  initiated  under
Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955,
shall be proceeded with and if the petitioner
resiles from her consent before the Family Court,
appropriate proceedings shall be taken against
her;  meaning  perjury.  The  High  Court  also
directed an exemplary cost of Rs.5,00,000/- to be
imposed on the petitioner and directed it to be
paid to two entities, one established in the care

--- Page 312 ---
3
of women and the other, a fund established for
poor patients. 
5. We are perfectly in agreement with the High
Court that such nefarious practices undermining
the judicial system has to be deprecated in the
strongest  of  terms.  Only  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case, we modify the order to
the extent of deleting the penalty imposed on the
petitioner; but cautioning her in the strongest
of  terms  from  indulging  in  such  activities
hereinafter. 
6. Insofar as the settlement is concerned, we
confirm the order of the High Court which made it
unenforceable against the party respondent. 
7. As far as the proceedings before the Family
Court,  we  deem  it  fit,  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case, to grant divorce to
the parties invoking our powers under Article 142
of the Constitution of India, finding from the
facts  and  circumstances,  an  irretrievable
breakdown of marriage.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of
with the above directions.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2283/2014
PENDIL RAVINDER                                   Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. The present Criminal Appeal has been filed against the
judgment of conviction dated 01.05.2007 passed by the First
Additional Session Court, Karimnagar convicting the appellant
for the offences punishable under sections 302 and 411 of
Indian Penal Code. The judgment of conviction dated 01.05.2007
has been affirmed in Criminal Appeal No. 924/2007 by the High
Court of Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad.
2. The  conviction  of  the  appellant  is  based  on
circumstantial evidence. As per the prosecution case one Mada
Devender Reddy who was known to the accused was last seen with
the accused on 13.09.2005 along with the cash of Rs. 50,000/-
(Rs. Fifty thousand only). They went to Bhulaxmi Lodge on
14.09.2005 and stayed in a room. The Management of the lodge
noticed the death of the deceased in the room and the matter
was investigated.
3. There is an evidence of last seen together and the
witnesses supported the same. The appellant has also been

--- Page 328 ---
2
identified by the witnesses because as many as 19 witnesses
were examined and there is a recovery of money which as per
the prosecution case, belong to the deceased. As the chain of
events  is  complete,  the  Trial  Court  has  convicted  the
appellant  and  thereafter  the  High  Court  affirmed  this
conviction.
4. In the present case, life imprisonment was awarded to the
appellant for the offences punishable under Section 302 IPC
and  03  years  rigorous  imprisonment  was  awarded  for  the
offences punishable under Section 411 of IPC.
5. The order passed by the learned Sessions Judge reveals
that the appellant was arrested on 10.10.2005 at 06:00 a.m.
and he is in custody since then, meaning thereby he is behind
bars for more than 20 years.
6. We do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment
of conviction passed by the Trial Court and affirmed by the
High Court. However, as the appellant has undergone the
sentence of more than 20 years, we are of the opinion that the
life imprisonment awarded to the appellant deserves to be
reduced to the period of sentence already undergone. Ordered
accordingly.
7. The appeal is partly allowed only to the extent of period
of the imprisonment.
8. The appellant is directed to be released forthwith if not
required in any other case.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026

AMIT KUMAR NANDI ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF U.P & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, Amit Kumar Nandi, is aggrieved by the grant of
regular bail to respondent No. 2, Sukanta Subrat Banerjee, by
the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow, vide  order
dated 09.04.2026 passed in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No.
2471/2026 in relation to First Information Report (FIR) No.
167/2019 dated 16.05.2019 registered with Police Station –
Mahanagar, District – Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, for offences
punishable under Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, 471, 504, 506 and
34 of the Indian Penal, Code, 1860.
3. It is an admitted fact that respondent No. 2, Sukanta Subrat
Banerjee, was absconding for over 6 years, during which period
he made various unsuccessful attempts to secure anticipatory
bail in relation to the aforestated FIR.  Further, we find that
respondent No. 2 approached the High Court by way of the bail
application,  in  which  he  was  immediately  granted  relief,
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 8824/2026     1

--- Page 332 ---
disclosing 6 past cases, in the first instance, and thereafter,
by  way  of  supplementary  affidavit  dated  08.04.2026,  he
disclosed 4 more cases registered against him.  However, it is
an admitted fact that 16 complaints/cases were registered
against respondent No. 2, Sukanta Subrat Banerjee, by that
time.
4. Given these circumstances, we are of the opinion that the High
Court was not justified in exercising discretion to grant bail
to respondent No. 2, Sukanta Subrat Banerjee, who was arrested
only on 05.12.2025 in relation to an FIR dating back to May,
2019.
5. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed, setting aside the impugned
order.
6. We are informed that respondent No. 2 was not released from
prison pursuant to the impugned order, as he had been arrested
in connection with another case.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13572/2015
UNION OF INDIA & ORS. APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
DILLIP KUMAR ROUT & ORS.            RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. In  the  Office  of  Principal  Accountant
General(A&E), Odisha, a Biometric Attendance System
was introduced with effect from 01.07.2013 vide
Circulars  dated  01.07.2013,  22.10.2013  and
06.11.2013.
3. These  Circulars  were  challenged  by  the
employees by filing an original application before
the Central Administrative Tribunal. The challenge
was turned down on the ground that the petition was
not maintainable as it does not relate to the
service condition.
4. Not  satisfied  by  the  said  order,  the
employees preferred a writ petition before the High
Court which was allowed by the impugned order dated
21.08.2014  on  the  ground  that  the  Circulars
introducing the Biometric Attendance System were
issued  without  prior  consultation  with  the

--- Page 340 ---
2
employees and were not in conformity with the
Swamy’s  Complete  Manual  on  Establishment  and
Administration for Central Government Offices.
5. In challenging the above order of the High
Court, the submission of learned counsel for the
appellant(s) is that the Swamy’s Complete Manual on
Establishment  and  Administration  for  Central
Government Offices nowhere contains any rules which
may have been formulated and followed by the Office
of  the  Principal  Accountant  General  (A&E)  and
therefore,  the  introduction  of  the  Biometric
Attendance System cannot be said to be in violation
of any rules of the Department. Furthermore, it has
been contended that the employees are not opposed
to the introduction of the Biometric Attendance
System as it is for the overall benefit of the
employees as well as the department.
6. Learned counsel for the respondents accepts
that  the  employees  are  not  opposed  to  the
introduction of the Biometric Attendance System.
7. Once the employees have no reservation on
the  introduction  of  the  Biometric  Attendance
System, we are of the opinion that no controversy
in this regard survives and the department can very
well go ahead with the implementation of the above
system.

--- Page 341 ---
3
8. Accordingly, the exercise undertaken by the
High Court appears to be totally unnecessary.
9. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of
the case, when the introduction of the Biometric
Attendance System is for the benefit of all the
stakeholders,  merely  for  the  reason  that  the
employees were not consulted before implementing
the same does not render the introduction of the
system to be illegal.
10. In the facts and circumstances, we allow the
appeal and set aside the order impugned passed by
the  High  Court  and  permit  the  Office  of  the
Principal Accountant General,(A&E) to implement the
Biometric Attendance System as envisaged by its
Circulars  dated  01.07.2013,  22.10.2013  and
06.11.2013.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Leave granted.
2. These appeals are filed against the common order in
revision by two of the revision applicants claiming parity
with another order insofar as the mesne profits granted is
concerned.
3. In the common order, we are concerned with Civil

--- Page 352 ---
Page 2 of 4
Revision Application (CRA) No.988 of 2014 to understand
the facts of which, Paragraph 9 of the impugned order is
extracted hereinunder:-
“9. Revision Applicant in CRA/988/2024 filed
Mesne Profit Application No.7 of 2005 against
the Respondent for recovery of the mesne
profit in respect of office No.603 admeasuring
about 1000 sq. ft. on sixth floor of Maker
Chamber No. IV, Nariman Point, Mumbai 400
021. The said application was allowed,
directing the Respondent to pay mesne profits
@ 12/- per sq. ft. per month from 01.01.2002
till actual delivery of possession along with
interest. Revision Applicant filed Misc. Appeal
No.539 of 2009 before the Appellate Bench
of Small Causes Court, which appeal was
dismissed under impugned judgment and
order dated 07.05.2014.”
4. The applicants before the High Court claimed parity
with the mesne profits granted in STC v. Neelam
Choudhary (CRA No.111 of 2019 decided on 16.10.2024).
However, the impugned order found that there should be
parity with STC v. Ravinder Singh (CRA No.308 of 2011,
decided on 28.11.2025). It was pointed out that in STC v.
Ravinder Singh, a rate of Rs.90 per sq. ft. per month was
granted, which was retained by this Court in an SLP filed
by the STC. The landlord therein had not filed for
enhancement, which was allowed in another case between

--- Page 353 ---
Page 3 of 4
STC v. Godavaridevi (CRA NO. 835 of 2014) awarding
Rs.150/- per sq. ft. per month.
5. The specific contention of the appellant herein is
seen from Paragraph 18 of the impugned order which is
extracted hereinunder: -
“18. In CRA 989/2014 and CRA/1010/2014,
possession was handed over by STC to
respective Applicants on 25.04.2011. In rest of
the matters, possession was handed over by
STC to respective Applicants on 01.03.2011.
Therefore, the period for which mesne profits
are awarded is from 01.01.2002 till 01.03.2011
or 25.4.2011. This Court, in the judgment of
STC Vs. Ravinder Singh (supra) has
considered the period from 01.10.2003 to
31.10.2010 which is a little shorter period than
the present group of petitions. In STC Vs.
Neelam Choudhary (supra), another learned
Single Judge of this Court has granted
Rs.150/- per sq. ft. per for a period between
September 2003 to December 2007 and
Rs.250/- per sq. ft. per from January 2008 till
August 2012.”
(underlining supplied by us for emphasis)
6. It is pointed out by Learned Counsel for the
appellant that the aforesaid determination of mesne profits
was challenged by STC in Special Leave Petition (C)
No.31033 of 2024, which was rejected by order dated
15.01.2025 and a review petition filed again by the STC

--- Page 354 ---
Page 4 of 4
was rejected by order dated 23.09.2025.
7. We hence modify the impugned order awarding
mesne profits as awarded in STC v. Neelam Choudhary,
emphasised by underlining in the above extract.
8. The appeals are allowed to the above extent.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        /2026
@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO.18363/2023
HIRA LAL DUBEY         APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.   RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The disciplinary proceedings initiated against the appellant and four
others ended in an order of dismissal being passed and not being successful in
the departmental appeal and revision, the appellant instituted a Writ Petition
(S) No.3597/2009 challenging the order of dismissal, order of the Appellate
Authority and order of the Revisional Authority. The learned Single Judge while
examining the appellant’s Writ Application had also heard similarly placed
applications in Writ Petition (S) Nos.4558/2008 and 4613/2008 and quashed
the order of punishment and other consequential orders and directed
reinstatement without backwages. Letters Patent Appeal No.841/2019 filed by
the appellant against the said order was belated, namely, it suffered from
delay of 771 days. Interlocutory Application filed for condonation of delay was
held to be not sufficiently explained and as such application for condonation of
1

--- Page 356 ---
delay was rejected. Consequently, the appeal was also dismissed whereas the
Letters Patent Appeals filed by other co-employees in Letters Patent Appeal
Nos.787/2018 and 112/2022 were allowed by condoning the delay and
consequently, the backwages were ordered to be paid.
4. The records would clearly disclose that the appeal filed by Jay Ram
Manjhi in Letters Patent Appeal No.787/2018 which was also belatedly filed,
namely, after 418 days was also allowed granting the backwages and Letters
Patent Appeal No.112/2022 was also allowed on parity with Jay Ram Manjhi,
whose appeal had been allowed and the order was expressly confined to them
alone. The appellant herein being similarly placed and appellant’s claim also
being similar to that of Jay Ram Manjhi’s plea put forward before the Appellate
Court, we are of the considered view that High Court committed an error in
ignoring the plea of the appellant. Hence, the impugned order cannot be
sustained. It is hereby set aside and appellant is ordered to be paid the
backwages as has been paid to Jay Ram Manjhi and others. Accordingly, the
appeal stands allowed. 
5. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to records. No order as
to costs.

SUMIT KAMLESH AMBHORE                              Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA                               Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 08.12.2025 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay rejecting the regular
bail prayer of the appellant in connection
with FIR No.141/2025, registered at P.S.
RCF, Mumbai.
4. The submission of the learned counsel
for the appellant is that the allegation of
stabbing the deceased is against co-accused
1

--- Page 364 ---
and  not  against  the  appellant.  He  also
contends that the CCTV footage of the spot
reveals that the appellant had not even
touched the deceased. In such circumstances,
it has been prayed that the appellant, who
has  suffered  incarceration  for  a  period
exceeding  one  year  pending  trial,  be
released on bail. 
5. The learned Counsel for the State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
by  submitting  that  the  appellant  has
previous criminal antecedents though it is
not disputed that no role of causing any
injury to the deceased is ascribed to the
appellant. 
6. Having regard to the above, without
expressing any opinion on the merits of the
case, we are of the view that the appellant
is entitled to be released on bail at this
stage.
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
The order passed by the High Court rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant is
2

--- Page 365 ---
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 02.05.2025
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna (briefly
the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the prayer of the
appellant for anticipatory bail.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in Teghra
Police Station Case No.404 of 2024, registered under
Sections 126(2), 127(2), 115(2), 121(2), 109, 303(2),
263, 62, 352, 351(3) and 3(5) of the  Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that one student
1

--- Page 384 ---
was caught by the teachers and by the Principal of a
school for carrying arms to the school. Police had come
to verify the information given by the school authority.
At that time, around 200 to 250 local persons gathered
near the school and tried to rescue the student. When the
informant tried to bring the accused student to the
police station in a police vehicle, it was resisted by
the crowd. Appellant was part of the crowd.
6. This Court by order dated 10.09.2025 had issued
notice and directed that no coercive action should be
taken  against  the  appellant  in  connection  with  the
aforesaid  case  subject  to  the  appellant  joining
investigation. Appellant was directed to appear before
the  Investigating  Officer  (IO)  on  17.09.2025  during
working hours or on any other date thereafter that may be
fixed by the IO.
7. In the counter affidavit filed by the State, it is
stated in paragraph 16 that appellant is in judicial
custody since 17.05.2026 in connection with another case
i.e., Fulwaria Police Station Case No.107/2026 registered
under Section 309(4) of the BNS. Appellant has also other
criminal antecedents.
8. Appellant has filed rejoinder affidavit wherein he
has stated that as directed by this Court vide the order
dated 10.09.2025, he had appeared before the IO on
17.09.2025. On a specific query by the Court learned
counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that  he  has  not
2

--- Page 385 ---
received any summons or notice from the Investigating
Officer  to  appear  in  the  investigation.  He  further
submits that much later he has been apprehended in the
other that is on 17.05.2026 for which he is taking
necessary steps as per law.
9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that in so far the
present case is concerned, appellant deserves to be
extended the benefit of pre-arrest bail.
10. Consequently, we set aside the order of the High
Court  dated  02.05.2025  and  make  our  order  dated
10.09.2025 absolute.
11. Appeal is accordingly disposed of.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
